book: After fifteen years of political estrangement following the election of 1800, former presidents John Adams (then seventy-six) and Thomas Jefferson (sixty-eight) renewed their friendship in January 1812 at the urging of their mutual friend Dr. Benjamin Rush. Over the next fourteen years—writing between Quincy, Massachusetts, and Monticello, Virginia—they debated natural aristocracy, religion, classics, American history, books, and old age right up to their final months in 1826.

Paul Wilstach selected and linked seventy-three letters from that reconciliation correspondence for The Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1925. This Paper Lanterns edition is transcribed from the unaugmented 1966 Capricorn Books reprint, keeping the editor's narrative bridges and the printed spelling and classical Greek and Latin quotations verbatim.

people.bio: Second President of the United States and leading theorist of constitutional balance, writing candidly in retirement from Quincy, Massachusetts, about history, classics, religion, and the American Revolution.
people.name: John Adams

people.bio: Principal author of the Declaration of Independence and third President of the United States, answering Adams from Monticello on philosophy, science, ancient Greek, and republican self-government.
people.name: Thomas Jefferson

people.bio: Philadelphia physician, educator, and signer of the Declaration of Independence whose long friendship with both statesmen helped bring about the 1812 reconciliation.
people.name: Benjamin Rush

people.bio: American author and editor who selected, arranged, and supplied connective commentary for this 1925 volume of the Adams–Jefferson correspondence.
people.name: Paul Wilstach

book: Alciphron, an imperial Greek epistolographer of the second or third century A.D., invented a lively fictive correspondence portraying everyday Athenian life and manners. Grouped into four vivid sections—Fishermen, Farmers, Parasites, and Courtesans—these 122 letters blend the humor of the Attic New Comedy of Menander with vivid glimpses of the Attic countryside, the Piraeus waterfront, parasitic dinner-hunters, and the intellectual and amorous rivalries of renowned hetairai.

Frederick Adam Wright (1869–1946), Professor of Classics at Birkbeck College, University of London, translated the complete extant collection with an introduction and notes for Routledge's prestigious Broadway Translations series in 1922 (co-published in New York by E. P. Dutton & Co.). Wright followed M. A. Schepers's definitive 1905 Teubner critical edition, rendering the witty character names into expressive English equivalents while preserving the charm, dramatic monologues, and classical allusions of the original Greek.

people.bio: Greek rhetorician and epistolary stylist whose fictional letters vividly depict the everyday world of Attic fishermen, rustic farmers, witty parasites, and famous courtesans.

people.name: Praxiteles

people.bio: Chief dramatist of Athenian New Comedy, whose fictional epistolary romance with Glycera forms the centerpiece of Alciphron's Courtesans.
people.name: Menander

people.bio: Athenian courtesan and companion of Menander, portrayed in Alciphron's correspondence declining an invitation from King Ptolemy of Egypt to remain in Athens.
people.name: Glycera

book: Anandabai Joshee (1865–1887) sailed from Calcutta to Philadelphia in 1883 to earn her medical degree at the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania, becoming the first Indian woman to qualify in Western medicine; her letters home trace the loneliness, winter cold, and steady resolve of those years before her death in Pune at twenty-one.

Caroline Wells Healey Dall assembled this biography and correspondence for Roberts Brothers in Boston in 1888, setting Joshee’s own words inside the circle of American and Indian reformers who followed her voyage.

book: The early correspondence of Aurelius Augustine (354–430), Bishop of Hippo Regius in Roman North Africa, spans his philosophical retirement at Cassiciacum, his ordination as presbyter and consecration as bishop, and his sustained pastoral and theological controversies with Donatists, Manichæans, and Pelagians. Volume I of this translation covers Letters I through XCIII (A.D. 386–408), including intimate exchanges with Nebridius, Romanianus, Paulinus of Nola and Therasia, Alypius, and Jerome on Scripture, liturgy, monastic discipline, and civic ethics.

Translated into English by the Rev. J. G. Cunningham, M.A. (1835–1907), under the general editorship of the Rev. Marcus Dods, M.A. (1834–1909), for T. & T. Clark's 'Works of Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo' (Vol. VI, Edinburgh, 1872; scan leaves 7–9). The Table of Contents (scan leaves 15–16, pp. xi–xii) lists 83 translated letters (with editorial summaries for omitted Letters 12, 24, 32, 45, 49, 52, 56, 57, 70, and 80) ending at Letter XCIII (scan leaf 456, p. 440). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Cunningham's preface, editorial headnotes, ligatures, polytonic Greek, scriptural and historical footnotes, and epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Bishop of Hippo Regius in Roman North Africa (395–430), theologian, and Doctor of the Church, whose Confessions, City of God, and extensive correspondence shaped Latin Christianity.
people.name: Saint Augustine of Hippo

people.bio: Scottish Free Church minister of Lochwinnoch (later of St. Luke's, Edinburgh) who translated the two-volume selection of St. Augustine's Letters (Vols. VI and XIII) for T. & T. Clark's series.
people.name: Rev. John George Cunningham

people.bio: Scottish Presbyterian theologian, New Testament scholar, and Principal of New College, Edinburgh, who served as general editor of T. & T. Clark's English translation of the Works of Aurelius Augustine.
people.name: Rev. Marcus Dods

people.bio: Christian priest, confessor, theologian, and translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible, with whom Augustine maintained a frank and learned correspondence over scriptural interpretation and the Septuagint.
people.name: Saint Jerome

people.bio: Roman senator, poet, and Bishop of Nola who, with his wife Therasia, corresponded warmly with Augustine on asceticism, Scripture, and ecclesiastical affairs.
people.name: Saint Paulinus of Nola

people.bio: Lifelong friend of Augustine from Thagaste, companion in Milan and Cassiciacum, and Bishop of Thagaste.
people.name: Saint Alypius of Thagaste

people.bio: Carthaginian friend and philosophical interlocutor of Augustine during his Milanese conversion and early African retirement, represented in Letters III–XIV.
people.name: Nebridius

people.bio: Bishop of Carthage and primate of North Africa, close collaborator of Augustine in African church councils and anti-Donatist and anti-Pelagian synods.
people.name: Aurelius of Carthage

book: Volume II of the Letters of Saint Augustine (Vol. XIII of T. & T. Clark's 'Works of Aurelius Augustine,' edited by the Rev. Marcus Dods and published in Edinburgh in November 1875; scan leaves 7, 9–11) completes the Rev. J. G. Cunningham's English translation of the correspondence of Augustine, Bishop of Hippo. Spanning Benedictine Letters XCV through CCLXIX (A.D. 408–429), this volume captures Augustine's mature theological, pastoral, and civic engagement across late Roman North Africa and the wider Mediterranean world.

As explained in the Prefatory Note (scan leaves 13–14, p. vi), Cunningham and Dods selected 160 of the 272 letters in the Benedictine edition across Volumes I and II, excluding letters already covered in the series' Donatist, anti-Pelagian, and Trinitarian volumes. Volume II presents 76 numbered items in the Table of Contents (scan leaves 15–16, pp. vii–viii)—75 translated letters plus Letter CCXIII, Augustine's official ecclesiastical record (gesta) designating Eraclius as his successor—including Augustine's celebrated exchanges with St. Jerome on Scripture and the origin of the soul, Flavius Marcellinus on Christianity and the Roman state after the sack of Rome, Count Boniface, Anicia Faltonia Proba on prayer, Evodius of Uzalis, and Possidius, followed by five scholarly indices (scan leaves 483–496, pp. 467–480).

people.bio: Bishop of Hippo Regius in Roman North Africa, theologian, and Doctor of the Church, whose correspondence addresses biblical exegesis, pastoral care, imperial politics, and the Pelagian and Donatist controversies.
people.name: Saint Augustine of Hippo

people.bio: Scottish Free Church minister of Lochwinnoch (later of St. Luke's, Edinburgh) who translated the two-volume selection of St. Augustine's Letters for T. & T. Clark's series.
people.name: Rev. John George Cunningham

people.bio: Scottish Presbyterian theologian, New Testament scholar, and Principal of New College, Edinburgh, who served as general editor of T. & T. Clark's English translation of the Works of Aurelius Augustine.
people.name: Rev. Marcus Dods

people.bio: Christian priest, confessor, theologian, and translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible, with whom Augustine maintained a frank and learned correspondence over scriptural interpretation and the origin of the soul.
people.name: Saint Jerome

people.bio: Roman imperial tribune and notary sent to Africa by Emperor Honorius to preside over the Conference of Carthage (411), and a close friend to whom Augustine dedicated De Civitate Dei and several major letters.
people.name: Flavius Marcellinus

people.bio: Fellow townsman and lifelong friend of Augustine from Thagaste who became Bishop of Uzalis and corresponded with Augustine on the nature of the soul and Christ's descent into hell.
people.name: Evodius of Uzalis

people.bio: Roman Christian noblewoman of the Anicii family who fled to North Africa after the 410 sack of Rome and received Augustine's celebrated treatise-letter on prayer (Letter CXXX).
people.name: Anicia Faltonia Proba

people.bio: Roman general and Comes Africae whose military campaigns, personal grief, and political turmoil prompted Augustine's counsel on Christian duty and loyalty.
people.name: Count Bonifacius

book: In November 1925 Madeleine Slade—the daughter of a British rear-admiral who had read Romain Rolland’s life of Gandhi in Paris—stepped off a train in Ahmedabad to join Sabarmati Ashram. For the next twenty-three years, from ashrams, third-class railway carriages, Yeravda prison, and London conference rooms, Gandhi wrote to her as ‘Mira’. The letters range without seam from carding cotton, boiling drinking water, and curing fevers to solitude, anger, prayer, and the dismantling of an empire.

Mirabehn edited and introduced this collection herself for Navajivan Publishing House in 1949, the year after Gandhi’s assassination. Because he answered her steadily even during fasts and national campaigns, the book reads like a private ledger of his daily discipline.

people.bio: Lawyer, writer, and leader of the Indian independence movement. He rose before dawn to answer correspondents by hand, treating an ordinary postcard with the same moral attention as a dispatch to the Viceroy.
people.name: M. K. Gandhi

people.bio: Englishwoman who left London for Sabarmati Ashram in 1925, spun her own cloth, accompanied Gandhi to the 1931 Round Table Conference, and kept these letters intact through decades of travel and imprisonment.
people.name: Mirabehn (Madeleine Slade)

book: Between 1876 and his death in 1897, Johannes Brahms carried on one of the most revealing musical correspondences of the nineteenth century with composer Heinrich von Herzogenberg and his gifted wife Elisabet, whose ear Brahms trusted above almost any other’s. Sending manuscripts bar by bar before publication, Brahms drew out Elisabet’s fearless, affectionate, and technically exact criticism alongside daily news of concerts, friends, and travel across Vienna, Leipzig, and Switzerland.

Edited in German by Brahms’s biographer Max Kalbeck and translated into English by Hannah Bryant for E. P. Dutton in 1909, the volume preserves nearly three hundred letters, musical incipits in notation, and Kalbeck’s concert notes.

people.bio: German composer, pianist, and conductor who treated Elisabet von Herzogenberg as one of his keenest private critics, often sending her new symphonies and songs in proof.
people.name: Johannes Brahms

people.bio: Pianist, singer, and composer of acute musical judgment whose candid bar-by-bar appraisals of Brahms’s manuscripts sit at the heart of this correspondence.
people.name: Elisabet von Herzogenberg

people.bio: Austrian composer, conductor of the Leipzig Bach-Verein, and later professor at the Berlin Hochschule, whose devotion to Bach and polyphony shaped a twenty-year friendship with Brahms.
people.name: Heinrich von Herzogenberg

people.bio: Music critic, librettist, and Brahms’s standard biographer, who edited these letters and supplied the historical and score-reference notes.
people.name: Max Kalbeck

book: Through the year 1809, Thomas Duer Broughton commanded the British Resident’s escort inside the mobile military camp of Daulat Rao Sindhia—a tented city of soldiers, merchants, courtiers, elephants, and camp followers shifting across Rajputana and central India. Writing home to his brother, he set down what passed outside his tent: Holi celebrations, court etiquette, unpaid cavalry mutinies, revenue raids, monsoon marches, and street theatre.

First issued in London in 1813 with hand-coloured plates, the letters were reprinted by Archibald Constable in 1892 with an introduction by Mountstuart Elphinstone Grant Duff. Read with an eye to its colonial vantage point, it remains an unusually vivid eyewitness record of late Maratha court life.

people.bio: East India Company officer and Persian scholar who fought at Seringapatam before joining the Residency at Sindhia’s camp. He later published one of the earliest English anthologies of Hindustani verse.
people.name: Thomas Duer Broughton

people.bio: Scottish Liberal politician, Governor of Madras (1881–1886), and diarist who supplied the historical introduction to this 1892 reprint.
people.name: Mountstuart Elphinstone Grant Duff

book: Opening in 68 B.C. in the thirty-ninth year of Cicero's life and running through 52 B.C., Volume I of Evelyn S. Shuckburgh's chronological translation captures the rise and crisis of Marcus Tullius Cicero's public career: his early letters to Atticus from Rome, the silence of his consulship in 63 B.C., the aftermath of the Catilinarian conspiracy, the formation of the First Triumvirate, his bitter exile to Thessalonica and Dyrrhachium in 58–57 B.C., his triumphant return, and his reluctant accommodation with Caesar and Pompey.

Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh (1843–1906), classical scholar and Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, translated Cicero's whole extant correspondence in chronological order for George Bell and Sons (first issued 1899–1900; this G. Bell and Sons, Ltd. Vol. I printing dated 1920 on scan leaf 7). Volume I contains 181 numbered letters (I–CLXXXI), Shuckburgh's general Introduction on Cicero's life and correspondence, Quintus Cicero's De Petitione Consulatus (Commentariolum Petitionis), and Appendices A–C (including early letters to Tiro). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Shuckburgh's historical introductions, outer-margin consular notes, classical Greek and Latin quotations, textual footnotes, and authentic epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Roman orator, statesman, philosopher, and consul of 63 B.C. whose surviving letters begin in 68 B.C. and chronicle his political ascent, exile in 58–57 B.C., and entanglement with the First Triumvirate.
people.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero

people.bio: English classical scholar, translator, and Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, who produced the first comprehensive chronological English translation of Cicero's letters alongside translations of Polybius and works on Roman history.
people.name: Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh

people.bio: Roman eques, banker, and publisher, lifelong intimate friend and confidant of Cicero, to whom Cicero addressed the majority of the letters in Volume I.
people.name: Titus Pomponius Atticus

people.bio: Younger brother of Marcus Cicero, praetor in 62 B.C., governor of Asia, and legate to Caesar in Gaul; author of the De Petitione Consulatus included in Volume I.
people.name: Quintus Tullius Cicero

people.bio: Cicero's first wife, to whom he wrote poignant letters from exile in Thessalonica and Dyrrhachium in 58 B.C. (Fam. XIV. 1–4).
people.name: Terentia

people.bio: Renowned Roman general and statesman ('Pompey the Great'), partner in the First Triumvirate with Caesar and Crassus, whose shifting political support shaped Cicero's exile and recall.
people.name: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus

people.bio: Roman consul of 57 B.C. who championed Cicero's recall from exile and subsequently governed Cilicia, receiving major political letters from Cicero in 56–54 B.C. (Fam. I. 1–9).
people.name: Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther

people.bio: Roman jurist whom Cicero recommended to Julius Caesar in Gaul and teased affectionately in a lively series of letters (Fam. VII. 6–18).
people.name: Gaius Trebatius Testa

book: In May 51 B.C., Marcus Tullius Cicero reluctantly departed Rome to serve as proconsul of Cilicia, an expansive province encompassing southeastern Asia Minor and Cyprus. Over the next two years, his correspondence vividly captures his clean provincial governance, border warfare against Parthian raiders and mountain tribes on Mount Amanus (where his troops hailed him Imperator), his constant craving for political intelligence from Rome, and the dramatic unraveling of the Roman Republic as Julius Caesar and Gnaeus Pompeius drifted into civil war.

Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh (1843–1906), classical scholar and late Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, translated the whole extant correspondence of Cicero in strict chronological order for George Bell and Sons between 1899 and 1900. Volume II collects 222 letters (Letters CLXXXII through CCCCIII) covering the crucial years 51 to 49 B.C. This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Shuckburgh's historical introductions, Roman calendar datelines, classical Greek and Latin quotations, textual footnotes, and authentic epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Roman orator, statesman, philosopher, and consul of 63 B.C. whose intimate correspondence during his Cilician proconsulship and the outbreak of Caesar's Civil War provides an unparalleled firsthand record of late Roman Republican politics.
people.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero

people.bio: English classical scholar, translator, and Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, who produced the first comprehensive chronological English translation of Cicero's letters alongside translations of Polybius and works on Roman history.
people.name: Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh

people.bio: Roman eques, banker, and publisher, lifelong intimate friend and confidant of Cicero, to whom Cicero addressed hundreds of letters discussing private finances, literary works, and state affairs.
people.name: Titus Pomponius Atticus

people.bio: Roman politician, orator, and curule aedile who maintained a witty, gossipy, and insightful political correspondence with Cicero in Cilicia, keeping him informed of senate debates and Caesar's maneuvers.
people.name: Marcus Caelius Rufus

people.bio: Roman general, statesman, and writer whose crossing of the Rubicon in January 49 B.C. ignited the Great Roman Civil War against Pompey and the Senate.
people.name: Gaius Julius Caesar

people.bio: Renowned Roman general and statesman ('Pompey the Great') who led the senatorial faction against Caesar in the Civil War of 49–48 B.C.
people.name: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus

people.bio: Roman senator and Stoic philosopher ('Cato the Younger'), renowned for unbending integrity and stubborn defence of the Republic against Caesar and Pompey.
people.name: Marcus Porcius Cato

people.bio: Roman patrician, consul of 54 B.C. and Cicero's predecessor as governor of Cilicia, with whom Cicero conducted a tense and formal correspondence concerning provincial restitution and augural lore.
people.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher

book: Following Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus in 48 B.C., Marcus Tullius Cicero spent a miserable year at Brundisium awaiting Julius Caesar's pardon, then returned to Rome under Caesar's dictatorship. Between 46 and February 44 B.C.—shadowed by divorce from Terentia, the death of his beloved daughter Tullia, and the eclipse of Republican liberty—Cicero turned to intense philosophical and rhetorical composition while corresponding with Republican exiles, Caesarian partisans, and lifelong confidants.

Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh (1843–1906), classical scholar and late Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, translated Cicero's whole extant correspondence in chronological order for George Bell and Sons (1899–1900). Volume III (published 1900; scan leaves 9, 11–14) collects 292 numbered letters (Letters CCCCIV through DCXCV, scan leaves 33–394) covering 48 to February 44 B.C., together with Appendix A (undated letters of recommendation, scan leaves 395–400) and Appendix B (chronological dates in Cicero's life, scan leaves 401–414). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Shuckburgh's historical introduction, Roman calendar datelines, classical Greek and Latin quotations, textual footnotes, and authentic epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Roman orator, statesman, philosopher, and consul of 63 B.C. whose letters of 48–44 B.C. chronicle his return to Rome after Pharsalus, private grief at Tullia's death, and life under Caesar's dictatorship.
people.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero

people.bio: English classical scholar, translator, and Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, who produced the first comprehensive chronological English translation of Cicero's letters alongside translations of Polybius and works on Roman history.
people.name: Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh

people.bio: Roman eques, banker, and publisher, lifelong intimate friend and confidant of Cicero, to whom Cicero wrote almost daily during 45 B.C. following Tullia's death.
people.name: Titus Pomponius Atticus

people.bio: Roman general, dictator, and statesman who pardoned Cicero after Pharsalus and whose autocratic rule forms the political backdrop of Volume III up to February 44 B.C.
people.name: Gaius Julius Caesar

people.bio: Roman jurist, consul of 51 B.C., and proconsul of Achaia, author of the famous letter of consolation to Cicero upon Tullia's death in 45 B.C. (Fam. IV, 5).
people.name: Servius Sulpicius Rufus

people.bio: Roman senator and consul of 51 B.C. who went into voluntary exile at Mytilene after Pharsalus, was pardoned by Caesar in 46 B.C., and was murdered at Piraeus on his return journey.
people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus

people.bio: Roman senator and general who corresponded with Cicero on philosophy and politics under Caesar's dictatorship before helping lead the conspiracy of the Ides of March.
people.name: Gaius Cassius Longinus

people.bio: Roman senator, Stoic-Academic philosopher, and close literary correspondent of Cicero, to whom Cicero dedicated major philosophical and rhetorical treatises in 46–45 B.C.
people.name: Marcus Junius Brutus

people.bio: Cicero's freedman, confidential secretary, and literary executor, to whom Cicero wrote affectionate letters concerning his health, household, and library.
people.name: Marcus Tullius Tiro

people.bio: Cicero's first wife of three decades, whose correspondence with Cicero in 48–47 B.C. reflects the strain of the civil war and precedes their divorce.
people.name: Terentia

book: Following the assassination of Julius Caesar on the Ides of March, 44 B.C., Marcus Tullius Cicero returned to the center of Roman political life, rallying the Senate against Mark Antony through his Philippic orations and an intense correspondence with the Republican generals in the provinces. Across 44 and 43 B.C., these letters—exchanged with Atticus, Decimus Brutus, Marcus Brutus, Cassius, Lucius Munatius Plancus, and Gaius Asinius Pollio—chronicle the fragile senatorial coalition, the Siege of Mutina, Octavian's march on Rome, and the formation of the Second Triumvirate.

Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh (1843–1906), classical scholar and late Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, translated the whole extant correspondence of Cicero in chronological order for George Bell and Sons between 1899 and 1900 (title leaf, scan leaf 9). Volume IV collects Letters DCXCVI (scan leaf 53, p. 1) through DCCCCXI (scan leaf 378, p. 326), together with Mark Antony's letter to Hirtius and Octavian from the Thirteenth Philippic (Preface, scan leaf 11, p. v), the Appendix letter of Pseudo-Cicero to Octavian (scan leaves 381–385, pp. 329–333), and the General Index to Volumes I–IV (scan leaves 387–438, pp. 335–386). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Shuckburgh's introduction, Roman calendar datelines, Greek and Latin quotations, textual footnotes, and authentic epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Roman orator, statesman, philosopher, and consul of 63 B.C. who led the senatorial opposition to Mark Antony in 44–43 B.C. before being proscribed and executed by the Second Triumvirate.
people.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero

people.bio: English classical scholar, translator, and Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, who produced the first comprehensive chronological English translation of Cicero's letters alongside translations of Polybius and works on Roman history.
people.name: Evelyn Shirley Shuckburgh

people.bio: Roman eques, banker, and publisher, lifelong intimate friend and confidant of Cicero, to whom Cicero addressed hundreds of letters discussing private finances, literary works, and state affairs.
people.name: Titus Pomponius Atticus

people.bio: Roman general, governor of Cisalpine Gaul, and one of the assassins of Julius Caesar, who held Mutina against Mark Antony during the winter of 44–43 B.C. and corresponded frequently with Cicero.
people.name: Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus

people.bio: Roman senator and leader of the Liberatores who assassinated Julius Caesar in 44 B.C., later commanding Republican forces in Macedonia and Greece.
people.name: Marcus Junius Brutus

people.bio: Roman senator, general, and co-leader with Marcus Brutus of the conspiracy against Julius Caesar, who secured Syria and the eastern provinces for the Republican cause in 43 B.C.
people.name: Gaius Cassius Longinus

people.bio: Roman senator and governor of Gallia Comata in 44–43 B.C. whose dispatches to Cicero and the Senate document his shifting allegiance during the Mutina campaign.
people.name: Lucius Munatius Plancus

people.bio: Roman politician and general ('Mark Antony'), consul with Caesar in 44 B.C., who sought to succeed to Caesar's power, besieged Decimus Brutus at Mutina, and formed the Second Triumvirate in 43 B.C.
people.name: Marcus Antonius

people.bio: Julius Caesar's adopted son and heir ('Octavian', later Emperor Augustus), whose rapid rise in 44–43 B.C. first allied him with Cicero and the Senate against Antony before his pact with Antony and Lepidus.
people.name: Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus

book: When Hernán Cortés sailed from Cuba in 1519 without his governor’s leave, his legal survival depended on convincing the nineteen-year-old Emperor Charles V that the prize justified the disobedience. His Cartas de relación—the first dispatches appear in this volume—combine field report, astonished inventory of Tenochtitlan’s markets and causeways, and cool political self-justification.

Francis Augustus MacNutt translated and annotated the series for G. P. Putnam’s Sons in 1908. This opening volume sets the early letters beside a biographical sketch, Cortés’s last will and testament, and a bibliography of the sixteenth-century printings.

people.bio: Spanish conquistador who led the campaign that overturned the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521. His five dispatches to Charles V became Europe’s primary account of the conquest of Mexico.
people.name: Hernán Cortés

people.bio: American diplomat and historian of early Spanish America who prepared the first complete English translation of all five letters of relation.
people.name: Francis Augustus MacNutt

book: At the heart of this volume sits the letter Dostoevsky wrote to his brother Michael on the evening of 22 December 1849, hours after standing blindfolded in a white shroud on Semjonovsky Square waiting for a firing squad that never shot. Around it stretch forty years of correspondence: engineering school in Petersburg, four silent years in the convict barracks at Omsk, exile in Siberia, pawnshops in Baden-Baden, and the feverish writing of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

Ethel Colburn Mayne translated this selection in 1914 from Alexander Eliasberg’s German edition, giving English readers their first sustained look at Dostoevsky off the page of his novels. Recollections by friends and a chronological table of his life close the book.

people.bio: Russian novelist and journalist whose years in Siberian prison broke his health and remade his imagination. His letters are headlong, candid about debt and epilepsy, and written mostly against impossible deadlines.
people.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky

people.bio: Irish biographer, short-story writer, and translator of Byron, Nietzsche, and Dostoevsky whose 1914 volume shaped how English-speaking readers first heard Dostoevsky’s voice.
people.name: Ethel Colburn Mayne

book: After the Russian archives opened in 1917, a cache of Dostoevsky’s papers emerged that earlier editors had cut or suppressed. Here are the unexpurgated letter from the Peter and Paul Fortress, long political and literary letters to the poet Apollon Maikov from Geneva and Dresden, reminiscences by his second wife Anna Grigoryevna, and the breathless dispatches he sent home to her from the 1880 Pushkin Celebration in Moscow—months before he died.
Translated straight from the Russian by S. S. Koteliansky and J. Middleton Murry in 1923, it serves as the sharper, more intimate companion to Ethel Colburn Mayne’s 1914 collection.

people.bio: Russian novelist whose late letters to Maikov and to his wife catch him balancing gambling ruin, homesickness in Europe, and the architecture of his last four novels.
people.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky

people.bio: Young stenographer hired to take down The Gambler in twenty-six days. She married Dostoevsky in 1867, rescued him from creditors, became his publisher, and kept his archive alive.
people.name: Anna Dostoevskaya

people.bio: Ukrainian-born translator and English critic whose 1920s collaborations brought Russian notebooks, letters, and memoirs directly from newly published Moscow texts into English.
people.name: S. S. Koteliansky & J. Middleton Murry

book: Long before the East India Company governed a single acre of India, its servants were merchants clinging to rented warehouses at Bantam, Surat, Mocha, and the Spice Islands, waiting on monsoon winds and royal permission to trade. These dispatches from 1602 to 1613—written in salty Jacobean English—report shipwrecks, Dutch and Portuguese skirmishes, pepper prices, and the first fumbling English embassies to the Mughal court.

Frederick Charles Danvers, Registrar of the India Office, opened this six-volume transcription of the Company’s ‘Original Correspondence’ in London in 1896, preserving original spelling alongside a glossary of seventeenth-century trade terms.

people.bio: English joint-stock trading company chartered by Elizabeth I in 1600. In its first decade its factors operated as vulnerable foreign merchants competing for cloves, pepper, and textiles across the Indian Ocean.
people.name: East India Company

people.bio: India Office archivist and historian of the Portuguese in India who edited this opening volume before passing the series to William Foster.
people.name: Frederick Charles Danvers

book: Between 1613 and 1615 English factors secured their first permanent factory at Surat, sent buyers inland toward Ahmedabad, Agra, and Ajmer, and opened an unlikely outpost at Hirado in Japan. The letters trace Thomas Aldworth’s obstinate defence of the Surat post, naval clashes with Portuguese galleons off Swally, and William Adams’s dispatches from Tokugawa Japan.

Published in London in 1897, this was the first volume edited by William Foster, whose scrupulous introductions, notes, and glossaries turned the India Office records into a cornerstone of early modern Asian history.

people.bio: During 1613–1615 the Company’s factors worked across an arc stretching from the Red Sea and Gujarat to Java and Japan, entirely dependent on seasonal fleets and local court charters.
people.name: East India Company

people.bio: Historiographer to the India Office and editor of Volumes II–VI of Letters Received, followed by thirteen volumes of The English Factories in India.
people.name: Sir William Foster

book: In the single year 1615, Sir Thomas Roe landed at Surat as King James I’s first accredited ambassador to the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, while Nicholas Downton beat off a Portuguese fleet in the Swally roadstead. Dispatches from Surat, Ajmer, Masulipatam, Sumatra, and Japan follow indigo and calico buying inland and the Company’s first tentative probes toward Safavid Persia.
Edited by William Foster for Sampson Low in 1899, Volume III keeps the exact spelling and blunt commercial idiom of Jacobean factors dealing with Mughal governors, local brokers, and European rivals.

people.bio: By 1615 the Company was moving from single speculative voyages to permanent coastal and inland factories, pressing for formal protection at Jahangir’s court.
people.name: East India Company

people.bio: India Office archivist who annotated these manuscripts with provenance notes, cross-references, and appendices.
people.name: Sir William Foster

book: Through 1616 Sir Thomas Roe trailed Emperor Jahangir’s court at Ajmer and Mandu, trying to turn courtly gifts and patience into a lasting commercial treaty, while factors in Persia, Siam, and the Moluccas reported on silk, indigo, cloves, and hardening friction with the Dutch East India Company. Every page reflects the sheer lag of seventeenth-century distance, where a letter to London might wait eighteen months for an answer.
Edited by William Foster and published in London in 1900 from the India Office’s ‘Original Correspondence’ files.

people.bio: In 1616 the Company’s factors across Mughal India, Persia, and the Malay Archipelago faced aggressive Dutch competition and complex negotiations at imperial courts.
people.name: East India Company

people.bio: India Office historiographer whose editions opened the earliest surviving English commercial archives from Asia to modern historians.
people.name: Sir William Foster

book: By 1617 the Company’s surviving paperwork had grown so dense that six months filled a volume of its own. These dispatches from January to June—sent from Surat, Burhanpur, Agra, Isfahan, Bantam, and Hirado—record the Company’s first silk mission to Shah Abbas’s Persia, an armed stand-off with Dutch ships in the Banda Islands, and Roe’s dry, exasperated lobbying inside Jahangir’s travelling camp.
Edited by William Foster and published in London in 1901, complete with appendices and a detailed subject index.

people.bio: By early 1617 the Company ran interconnected factories across Mughal India, Safavid Persia, Java, and Japan, tied together by monsoon sailings and overland couriers.
people.name: East India Company

people.bio: Editor of Volumes II–VI of Letters Received, transcribing original seventeenth-century abbreviations, spelling, and endorsements without modernising them.
people.name: Sir William Foster

book: The closing half of 1617 brings the six-volume series to an end at a pivot point. As Dutch warships squeezed English factors out of the Banda spice trade, the Company’s centre of gravity shifted steadily toward Surat, Ahmedabad, and the Mughal interior—while everyday letters still pause over fevers, private debts, Persian silk, and life inside Indian cities.
Edited by William Foster and published in London in 1902. From 1618 onward, Foster carried the archive forward in his calendared series The English Factories in India.

people.bio: The second half of 1617 marked the turn away from the Spice Islands that eventually anchored the Company’s fortunes on the Indian subcontinent.
people.name: East India Company

people.bio: India Office historiographer who completed this six-volume transcription in 1902 before editing thirteen subsequent volumes on seventeenth-century India.
people.name: Sir William Foster

book: Volume I of Mabel Loomis Todd’s 1894 Roberts Brothers edition gathers Emily Dickinson’s correspondence from her Amherst schoolgirl years through the quiet, sharply observed letters of her adulthood, written to family members, friends, and mentors like Samuel Bowles and Thomas Wentworth Higginson.
Published eight years after Dickinson’s death, this first volume introduced readers to a prose voice as compressed, daring, and musical as her poems.

people.bio: American poet whose life in Amherst yielded nearly eighteen hundred poems and a correspondence as compressed, playful, and startling as her verse.
people.name: Emily Dickinson

people.bio: American editor and writer who transcribed and published the earliest posthumous editions of Emily Dickinson’s poems and letters in the 1890s.
people.name: Mabel Loomis Todd

book: For twenty-six years, Michael Faraday at the Royal Institution in London and the German-Swiss chemist Christian Friedrich Schoenbein in Basel swapped experiments, doubts, and family news across the Channel. In these letters (1836–1862) they argue over passive iron, ozone, gun-cotton, electromagnetism, and the nature of light—until, in the final years, Faraday writes with quiet dignity about his own failing memory and lays down his notebooks.

Georg W. A. Kahlbaum and Francis V. Darbishire edited the exchange for joint publication in Basel and London in 1899, keeping Schoenbein’s lively, slightly unidiomatic English intact alongside thorough chemical and historical notes.

people.bio: Bookbinder’s apprentice turned experimental physicist at the Royal Institution whose discoveries of electromagnetic induction and benzene laid the groundwork for electrical engineering and modern chemistry.
people.name: Michael Faraday

people.bio: Professor of chemistry at Basel, discoverer of ozone and gun-cotton (nitrocellulose), and one of Faraday’s warmest scientific confidants.
people.name: Christian Friedrich Schoenbein

book: From Pope Gregory VII’s 1075 rebuke of Emperor Henry IV to Robert Falcon Scott’s last pencil note in an Antarctic tent, this anthology collects moments when public history narrowed to a single sheet of paper. Columbus reporting the New World, Anne Boleyn writing from the Tower, Samuel Johnson turning down Lord Chesterfield’s late patronage, and Abraham Lincoln consoling Mrs. Bixby sit side by side in chronological order.
Curtis Gentry chose and introduced the letters for Thomas Y. Crowell in New York in 1930, prefacing each one with the immediate scene in which it was written.

people.bio: American educator and anthologist who assembled this volume for general readers, keeping the commentary short so the letters themselves carry the weight.
people.name: Curtis Gentry

book: Rediscovered in 1815 by Cardinal Angelo Mai on a palimpsest divided between the Ambrosian Library at Milan and the Vatican Library at Rome (Preface, scan leaf 13; Introduction, scan leaves 19–24), the correspondence of Marcus Cornelius Fronto (c. A.D. 100–c. 166/170) offers an intimate portrait of Roman literary and court life under the Antonines. Volume I spans A.D. 139–161 (scan leaves 67–373), preserving Fronto's letters to and from his imperial pupil Marcus Aurelius (as Caesar and as Emperor), alongside letters involving Antoninus Pius, Lucius Verus, Domitia Lucilla, Appian, Herodes Atticus, and Roman friends.

Charles Reginald Haines (1856–1935) edited the Latin and Greek text anew and produced this first English translation in 1919 (title leaf, scan leaf 11; Preface, scan leaf 13). Volume I includes Haines's Preface (scan leaves 13–14), Introduction and essay 'Fronto, the Orator and the Man' (scan leaves 17–50), Bibliography (scan leaves 51–59), Chronological Table (scan leaves 60–62), Sigla (scan leaf 63), and 152 translated letters and speeches across 154 English facing-page leaves (scan leaves 67–373). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Haines's historical apparatus, polytonic Greek quotations, textual footnotes, and authentic epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Roman grammarian, rhetorician, and consul suffectus of A.D. 143 (Chronological Table, scan leaf 61), born at Cirta in Numidia, who served as tutor in Latin rhetoric to Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.
people.name: Marcus Cornelius Fronto

people.bio: Roman emperor (r. A.D. 161–180) and Stoic philosopher, adopted by Antoninus Pius and made Caesar in A.D. 139, whose youthful correspondence with his rhetoric master Fronto fills the bulk of Volume I.
people.name: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus

people.bio: Roman emperor (r. A.D. 138–161), adoptive father of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, to whom Fronto addressed letters on his Asian proconsulship (scan leaf 301, p. 237).
people.name: Antoninus Pius

people.bio: Co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius (r. A.D. 161–169) and pupil of Fronto, who corresponded warmly with his former teacher.
people.name: Lucius Verus

people.bio: Mother of Marcus Aurelius and correspondent of Fronto, who exchanged Greek and Latin letters with her (scan leaf 79 fn. 1).
people.name: Domitia Lucilla

people.bio: Greek historian of Rome and friend of Fronto, who exchanged Greek letters with him on gifts and friendship.
people.name: Appian of Alexandria

people.bio: Athenian sophist, Roman consul of A.D. 143, and rhetoric tutor to Marcus Aurelius, reconciled with Fronto through Marcus's mediation.
people.name: Herodes Atticus

people.bio: English classical scholar who edited and produced the first English translation of Fronto's correspondence (2 vols., 1919–1920).
people.name: Charles Reginald Haines

book: Volume II of C. R. Haines's edition and translation of the Correspondence of Marcus Cornelius Fronto (first published 1920; revised and reprinted 1929, scan leaf 10) continues the letters between Fronto and Marcus Aurelius from 162 A.D. through the Parthian War and Fronto's correspondence with Lucius Verus, Antoninus Pius, and friends such as Praecilius Pompeianus, Arrius Antoninus, Claudius Julianus, and Aufidius Victorinus.

Alongside the main correspondence (pp. 1–247, scan leaves 13–259), this volume preserves Other Miscellaneous Remains of Fronto (pp. 249–285, scan leaves 261–297), Miscellaneous Letters of Marcus Aurelius with Haines's critical Introduction and Addendum (pp. 287–320, scan leaves 299–332), and the complete volume Indexes (Index of Names, Latin and Greek Index, Table of Matters, and Conspectus of Pages, pp. 321–371, scan leaves 333–383). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Haines's English translation, textual footnotes, classical quotations, and epistolary layouts verbatim.

people.bio: Roman grammarian, rhetorician, and consul suffectus in 143 A.D. from Cirta in Numidia; rhetoric tutor and lifelong correspondent of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.
people.name: Marcus Cornelius Fronto

people.bio: Roman Emperor (161–180 A.D.) and Stoic philosopher, whose intimate letters to and from his tutor Fronto illuminate his youth, family life, and early reign.
people.name: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus

people.bio: Co-emperor of Rome with Marcus Aurelius (161–169 A.D.) and commander during the Parthian War (162–166 A.D.), also a former pupil of Fronto.
people.name: Lucius Verus

people.bio: Daughter of Antoninus Pius and wife of Marcus Aurelius, featured in the Miscellaneous Letters of Marcus Aurelius during the revolt of Avidius Cassius (175 A.D., scan leaves 327–331).
people.name: Faustina the Younger

people.bio: Roman senator, consul, and praefectus urbi; fellow pupil of Fronto with Marcus Aurelius and husband of Fronto's daughter Gratia.
people.name: Aufidius Victorinus

people.bio: English classical scholar who edited and produced the first complete English translation of Fronto's correspondence (2 vols., 1919–1920; revised 1929).
people.name: Charles Reginald Haines

book: Gandhi treated the open letter to an adversary—always beginning ‘Dear Friend’—as a formal step of satyagraha: state your case plainly before acting. Gathered here are twenty-nine of his most consequential public letters from 1920 to 1943, including his return of the Kaisar-i-Hind medal, his March 1930 ultimatum to Lord Irwin on the eve of the Salt March, his wartime appeals to ‘Every Briton’ and to Adolf Hitler, and his exchanges with Viceroy Linlithgow from the Aga Khan Palace.
Compiled by R. L. Khipple and printed in Lahore in 1947—the year of Independence and Partition—preserving the contemporary framing in which these letters first reached Indian readers.

people.bio: Indian independence leader whose public letters turned formal colonial correspondence into a plain-spoken arena of moral argument.
people.name: M. K. Gandhi

book: Excavated from Old Babylonian clay tablets in southern Mesopotamia and preserved in the British Museum, the eighty-three cuneiform letters translated in this volume offer an immediate, unvarnished record of royal administration under the First Dynasty of Babylon in the eighteenth and seventeenth centuries B.C. (dated on the 1900 title page to 'about B.C. 2200' from Nabonidus's round figures before twentieth-century Mari and Venus-tablet chronology placed Hammurabi's reign at c. 1792–1750 B.C.; Introduction, scan leaves 80–81, pp. lxx–lxxi). Fifty-five royal dispatches pass directly from Hammurabi (Ḫammurabi) to Sin-idinnam, his high official in southern Babylonia at Larsam (Section I, scan leaves 85–198, pp. 3–116), directing troop movements (Letter I, scan leaf 85, p. 3), the conveyance and return of Elamite goddesses (Letters II–III, scan leaves 88–93, pp. 6–11), the insertion of an intercalary second Elul in the calendar (Letter IV, scan leaf 94, p. 12), the dredging of the Damanum and Erech canals (Letters V–VII, scan leaves 96–101, pp. 14–19), bribery inquiries and restitution against money-lenders (Letters VIII–XIII, scan leaves 102–114, pp. 20–32), temple and tax audits (Letters XIX–XXI, scan leaves 127–133, pp. 45–51), timber and grain convoys to Babylon (Letters XXII–XXVIII, scan leaves 134–148, pp. 52–66), royal sheep-shearing accounts (Letters XXX–XXXV, scan leaves 150–162, pp. 68–80), and arrest warrants for insubordinate officials (Letters LIII–LV, scan leaves 192–198, pp. 110–116). Sections II–VI add twenty-six royal letters of Hammurabi's successors—Samsu-iluna (6 letters, scan leaves 199–211, pp. 117–129), Abēšu’ / Abi-eshuh (13 letters, scan leaves 212–238, pp. 130–156), Ammiditana / Ammi-ditana (2 letters, scan leaves 239–243, pp. 157–161), and Ammizaduga / Ammi-saduqa (5 sheep-shearing summonses to Ibni-Sin, scan leaves 244–249, pp. 162–167)—addressed largely to the merchant guild (Kār-Sippar) and judges of Sippar, together with two Miscellaneous Letters involving Sin-idinnam, the court in Kutalla, and Sin-idinnam's wife Aḫatim (scan leaves 250–253, pp. 168–171).

Assyriologist Leonard William King, M.A., F.S.A. (1869–1919), Assistant in the Department of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities at the British Museum, edited the cuneiform autographs in Volumes I–II (1898–1900) and completed the work with Volume III: English Translations, etc., issued as Vol. VIII of Luzac’s Semitic Text and Translation Series (London: Luzac and Co., printed by Stephen Austin and Sons at Hertford, Preface dated September 1st, 1900; scan leaves 9–20). Alongside paired Akkadian transliterations (Obv./Rev.), line-numbered English translations, and historical headnotes for all eighty-three letters, Volume III contains the Frontispiece portrait sculpture of Hammurabi (Brit. Mus., No. 22,454; scan leaf 14), King's Introduction on Old Babylonian postal convoys, clay tablets and envelopes, greeting formulae, provincial administration, and First Dynasty chronology (scan leaves 27–81, pp. xix–lxxi), Royal Inscriptions of Hammurabi and later kings of the dynasty (Sections VII–IX, scan leaves 254–293, pp. 172–211), the Chronicle of the Kings of the First Dynasty (Section X, scan leaves 294–335, pp. 212–253), the Appendix (scan leaves 336–340, pp. 254–258), and complete Babylonian and Sumerian Vocabularies and Indices (scan leaves 341–417, pp. 259–335). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves King's Assyriological diacritics (Ḫ, Š, Ṣ, Ṭ, Ḳ, macrons), determinative superscripts, outer-margin shoulder notes, and critical footnotes verbatim.

Source Text & Copyright Provenance: Edited and translated by Leonard William King (1869–1919), published in London by Luzac and Co. in 1900 (digitized from Cornell University Library at Internet Archive as cu31924104781285). Published in 1900 by an editor-translator who died in 1919, this work is in the public domain worldwide.
