people.bio: Sixth Amorite king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (dated in King's 1900 edition to 'about B.C. 2200'; scan leaves 15, 80–81), conqueror of Rim-Sin of Larsa and promulgator of the Code of Hammurabi, whose fifty-five administrative and judicial letters to Sin-idinnam open this volume (scan leaves 85–198, pp. 3–116).
people.name: Hammurabi

people.bio: British Assyriologist, Assistant in the Department of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities at the British Museum and later Professor of Assyrian and Babylonian Archaeology at King's College London, who edited, transliterated, and translated this three-volume corpus of First Dynasty letters and inscriptions (scan leaves 15, 17–20).
people.name: Leonard William King

people.bio: High Babylonian royal administrator stationed at Larsam under Hammurabi (and bearer of a common Old Babylonian official name recurring in Sippar judicial dispatches under Samsu-iluna, Abi-eshuh, and Ammi-ditana; Introduction, scan leaves 34–36, pp. xxvi–xxviii; Letter LXXXIII, scan leaf 251, p. 169).
people.name: Sin-idinnam

people.bio: Seventh king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, son and successor of Hammurabi, represented here by six royal letters on fishing rights, temple grain, tax relief, and judicial administration at Sippar alongside his bilingual building inscription (scan leaves 199–211, 281–288; pp. 117–129, 199–206).
people.name: Samsu-iluna

people.bio: Eighth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (printed Abēšu’), son of Samsu-iluna, author of thirteen administrative and judicial letters to Sin-idinnam, Marduk-naṣir, the merchant guild (Kār-Sippar), and the judges of Sippar concerning canal floods, fugitive slaves, tribute, and corn harvests (scan leaves 212–238, pp. 130–156).
people.name: Abi-eshuh

people.bio: Ninth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (printed Ammiditana), son of Abi-eshuh, represented by two letters concerning grain shipments to Šamaš-natsir upon favourable omens and overdue shepherd tribute at Sippar-iaḫrurum (scan leaves 239–243, pp. 157–161).
people.name: Ammi-ditana

people.bio: Tenth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (printed Ammizaduga), son of Ammi-ditana, represented by five royal summonses ordering Ibni-Sin and other Sippar officials to attend the annual New Year sheep-shearing at the House of the New Year's Festival in Babylon (scan leaves 244–249, pp. 162–167).
people.name: Ammi-saduqa

people.bio: Keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities at the British Museum, general editor of Luzac's Semitic Text and Translation Series (scan leaf 10), who acquired many of the First Dynasty tablets in Babylonia and assisted King during the preparation of the work (Preface, scan leaf 20, p. xii).
people.name: E. A. Wallis Budge

book: In November 1847 the young botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker boarded the steam-frigate Sidon alongside the incoming Governor-General Lord Dalhousie, bound for Calcutta and the Himalayas. In four long, observant letters sent home from Madeira, Alexandria, Cairo, Suez, Aden, Ceylon, and Bengal, he sketches desert plants, coastal rock strata, shipboard boredom, and his first bewildered days on the Hooghly.
Privately printed in 1848 as extracts from his correspondence, these letters capture the raw field notes out of which his classic Himalayan Journals (1854) later grew.

people.bio: British botanist, explorer, and Director of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. Charles Darwin’s closest scientific confidant, he spent three years botanising in Sikkim, Nepal, and eastern Bengal.
people.name: Joseph Dalton Hooker

book: Published between 20 B.C. and c. 13 B.C. (Introduction, scan leaves 18–19, pp. xii–xiii), the twenty-three verse letters of Quintus Horatius Flaccus (Horace, 65–8 B.C.) transform the Roman poetic epistle into an intimate vehicle for ethical reflection, friendship, rural retirement, and literary criticism. Book I (twenty epistles, 20 B.C.; scan leaves 283–427, pp. 247–391) opens with Horace's farewell to lyric verse addressed to his patron Gaius Maecenas (Epist. I. i, scan leaves 284–295) and ranges across moral letters to young Maximus Lollius on reading Homer at Praeneste (I. ii, scan leaves 296–303), inquiries to Julius Florus on Tiberius's Eastern expedition (I. iii, scan leaves 305–309), console-and-counsel notes to the elegist Albius Tibullus (I. iv, scan leaves 311–313), a model letter of introduction to the future emperor Tiberius (I. ix, scan leaves 345–347), praise of Sabine country peace to Aristius Fuscus and to his own farm bailiff (I. x and I. xiv, scan leaves 349–355, 373–377), and the famous closing address to his own book (I. xx, scan leaves 423–427).

Book II (scan leaves 428–477, pp. 392–441) and the Ars Poetica or Epistle to the Pisos (scan leaves 478–525, pp. 442–489) present Horace's mature literary criticism: his defence of modern Roman poetry addressed to the Emperor Augustus (II. i, scan leaves 428–455), his reflections on poetic craft and philosophical old age to Julius Florus (II. ii, scan leaves 457–477), and his celebrated epistolary treatise on dramatic and poetic propriety addressed to Calpurnius Piso and his two sons (Ars Poetica, scan leaves 478–525). Translated into rhythmic English prose with analytical introductions to each epistle, explanatory footnotes, and an Index of Proper Names by Henry Rushton Fairclough (1862–1938), Professor of Classical Literature at Stanford University (first printed 1926, revised and reprinted 1929, London: William Heinemann Ltd.; prepared from the unmodified 1942 impression of the 1929 revised text, scan leaves 9–10, 13–14), this edition slice presents the complete English Epistles and Ars Poetica alongside Fairclough's Preface, General Introduction (scan leaves 13–36, pp. vii–xxx), and Index of Proper Names (scan leaves 527–545, pp. 491–509).

people.bio: Roman lyric poet, satirist, and epistolary philosopher, freedman's son of Venusia who fought under Brutus at Philippi before winning the friendship of Maecenas and receiving the Sabine farm in 33 B.C. (scan leaves 17, 427; pp. xi, 391).
people.name: Quintus Horatius Flaccus

people.bio: Henry Rushton Fairclough, Canadian-born classical scholar and Professor of Classical Literature at Stanford University (title leaf, scan leaf 9), who prepared the English prose translation, analytical epistle introductions, notes, and Index of Proper Names (Preface dated December 15, 1925 and February 4, 1929, scan leaf 14).
people.name: H. Rushton Fairclough

people.bio: Etruscan-descended Roman knight, trusted diplomatic adviser of Augustus, and literary patron of Virgil and Horace, who presented Horace with his Sabine estate in 33 B.C. and is addressed in Epistles I. i, I. vii, and I. xix (scan leaves 17, 284, 329, 415, 536).
people.name: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas

people.bio: First Roman Emperor (reigned 27 B.C.–A.D. 14), who gently reproached Horace for not addressing any of his conversational poems to him and thereby prompted Epistle II. i on the history and dignity of Roman literature (scan leaves 428, 433, 529).
people.name: Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus

people.bio: Young Roman orator, poet, and companion in the Eastern retinue of Tiberius Claudius Nero, to whom Horace addressed Epistle I. iii and the major literary letter Epistle II. ii (scan leaves 18, 305, 457, 533).
people.name: Julius Florus

people.bio: Young Roman student of rhetoric and veteran of Augustus's Cantabrian campaign (25–24 B.C.), probably eldest son of the consul Marcus Lollius (21 B.C.), addressed by Horace on Homer's moral wisdom in Epistle I. ii and on courtly independence in Epistle I. xviii (scan leaves 296, 402).
people.name: Maximus Lollius

people.bio: Roman elegiac poet and candid critic of Horace's Sermones, who died in 19 B.C. shortly after Virgil, addressed at his country retreat near Pedum in Epistle I. iv (scan leaves 311, 313, 527).
people.name: Albius Tibullus

people.bio: Stepson of Augustus and future Roman Emperor (A.D. 14–37), commander of the Eastern expedition of 20 B.C. mentioned in Epistles I. iii and I. xii, and recipient of Horace's deft letter of recommendation for Septimius in Epistle I. ix (scan leaves 18, 305, 345, 543).
people.name: Tiberius Claudius Nero

people.bio: A Roman nobleman and his two sons of the Calpurnian gens—identified either with Lucius Calpurnius Piso (consul 15 B.C., urban prefect A.D. 14) or Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso (consul 23 B.C., fellow-officer of Horace under Brutus) and his sons Gnaeus and Lucius—to whom Horace addressed the Ars Poetica (scan leaves 19, 478, 539–540).
people.name: The Pisos (Calpurnius Piso and Sons)

people.bio: Roman grammarian, writer of dramas, and intimate city-loving friend of Horace, to whom Horace praised the streams and woods of his Sabine farm in Epistle I. x (scan leaves 349, 351, 528).
people.name: Marcus Aristius Fuscus

people.bio: Philosophically minded friend of Horace and procurator of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa's estates in Sicily, to whom Horace commended Pompeius Grosphus and recounted contemporary Roman news in Epistle I. xii (scan leaves 363, 365, 534).
people.name: Iccius

book: Victor Hugo’s correspondence from 1815 to 1845 begins with a fourteen-year-old writing between separated parents and rises quickly through ardent courtship letters to Adèle Foucher, dispatches from the coronation of Charles X at Reims, and the battles of French Romanticism. Its sharpest drama lies in the long exchange with the critic Charles Augustin Sainte-Beuve—a close literary alliance slowly undone by jealousy and love.
Edited by Hugo’s devoted friend and literary executor Paul Meurice, and published in English by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in 1896 as the first of two volumes.

people.bio: French poet, playwright, and novelist—author of Notre-Dame de Paris and Les Misérables—who stood at the storm-centre of French Romanticism and nineteenth-century politics.
people.name: Victor Hugo

people.bio: French dramatist, journalist, and lifelong friend who handled Hugo’s publishing in Paris during his nineteen years of exile and later edited his letters.
people.name: Paul Meurice

book: Volume II follows Hugo from leisurely sketches along the Rhine into the rupture of Louis-Napoleon’s December 1851 coup d’état, flight to Brussels, and nineteen years of defiant exile on Jersey and Guernsey. From Hauteville House—refusing every imperial amnesty—he writes to Garibaldi, Mazzini, Baudelaire, Swinburne, and his children while finishing Les Misérables, before returning to Paris after the collapse of the Second Empire.
Edited by Paul Meurice and issued by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in 1898 as the companion to Volume I.

people.bio: During two decades on the Channel Islands, Hugo turned exile into a European pulpit—fighting capital punishment, defending the Paris Communards, and writing at full stretch.
people.name: Victor Hugo

people.bio: Hugo’s literary executor who arranged this second volume into four movements, from the Rhine journeys to Hugo’s final decade back in Paris.
people.name: Paul Meurice

book: In public, the elderly Alexander von Humboldt played the polite chamberlain at the Prussian court in Berlin; in private letters to the diplomat Karl August Varnhagen von Ense (1827–1858), he let the mask drop. Interleaved with Varnhagen’s own biting diary notes, the book is full of acid court gossip, quiet defences of harassed liberal scholars, and complaints about finishing his encyclopaedic Kosmos while half of Europe clamours at his door.

Published almost immediately after both men died, the unvarnished candour caused a scandal in Berlin and sold out across Europe. Friedrich Kapp translated this New York edition for Rudd & Carleton in 1860.

links.label: Karl August Varnhagen von Ense on Wikipedia

people.bio: Prussian naturalist, geographer, and explorer of South America who saw nature as an interconnected web and maintained one of the largest scientific correspondences of the nineteenth century.
people.name: Alexander von Humboldt

people.bio: Prussian diplomat, biographer, and husband of the salonnière Rahel Varnhagen, whose diaries preserve the sharper private talk of nineteenth-century Berlin.
people.name: Karl August Varnhagen von Ense

book: Spanning A.D. 354 to 363 from Julian's student days and his campaigns in Gaul as Caesar to his sole reign as Augustus and final Persian expedition, Volume III of Wilmer Cave Wright's edition and translation gathers Julian's extant correspondence alongside his polemical treatise Against the Galilaeans. The letters illuminate his philosophical circle (Priscus, Maximus of Ephesus, Iamblichus, Libanius, Oribasius), his religious reforms as Pontifex Maximus, his edicts on Christian teachers and Alexandrian civic affairs, and his private correspondence with family and officials.

Wilmer Cave Wright, Ph.D. (1868–1951), late of Girton College, Cambridge, and Professor of Greek in Bryn Mawr College, Pennsylvania (title leaf, scan leaf 9), published Volume III in 1923 (MCMXXIII). As detailed in the Contents (scan leaf 11), the volume comprises an Introduction to the Letters and Bibliography (pp. vii–lxvii), Letters 1–58 with Dates (pp. 3–209), Letters 59–73 Undated (pp. 209–237), Apocryphal Letters 74–83 (pp. 237–293), The Shorter Fragments 1–14 (pp. 295–303), Epigrams (pp. 305–309), Introduction to Against the Galilaeans (pp. 313–317), Against the Galilaeans Book I and Fragments (pp. 319–433), a Hertlein/Wright/Bidez-Cumont Table of Numbers (pp. 435–438), and an Index (pp. 439–448). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Wright's English translation, outer-margin chronological notes, polytonic Greek citations, textual footnotes, and concordance tables verbatim.

Source Text: Translated by Wilmer Cave Wright (1868–1951) and published in 1923 (The Works of the Emperor Julian, Vol. III, London: William Heinemann; New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, MCMXXIII; scan leaves 9–10). Published in 1923, this edition is in the public domain in the United States and in jurisdictions applying a life-plus-seventy-years copyright term; readers accessing this work from jurisdictions with longer post-mortem terms (such as eighty or one hundred years post mortem auctoris) should check applicable local copyright laws.

people.bio: Flavius Claudius Julianus, Roman Emperor (361–363), Neoplatonist philosopher, and author, whose extant letters and polemical treatise Against the Galilaeans survive in this third and final volume of his collected works.
people.name: Emperor Julian

people.bio: English-born classical scholar, alumna of Girton College, Cambridge, and Professor of Greek at Bryn Mawr College, who translated the three-volume edition of the Works of the Emperor Julian (1913–1923).
people.name: Wilmer Cave Wright

people.bio: Greek rhetorician and sophist of Antioch, close friend and correspondent of Emperor Julian.
people.name: Libanius

people.bio: Neoplatonist philosopher and theurgist, pupil of Aedesius, and Julian's spiritual mentor.
people.name: Maximus of Ephesus

people.bio: Greek medical writer and personal physician to Emperor Julian, whom he accompanied to Gaul and on the Persian campaign.
people.name: Oribasius

people.bio: Neoplatonist philosopher and friend of Julian, summoned to Gaul and later present at Julian's deathbed in Persia.
people.name: Priscus of Epirus

book: In the early 1920s a Trenton, New Jersey high-school English teacher named Sharpless Dobson Green asked his students to write to living scientists, writers, judges, inventors, and politicians—and over three hundred of them wrote back. Some sent stiff homilies, others unexpectedly candid notes on failure, reading, and how to spend a working life; taken together, they form an accidental self-portrait of public America in 1925.
Published by the Gregg Publishing Company in 1925, with brief contemporary biographies of the contributors appended at the back.

people.bio: English teacher at Trenton Senior High School who turned a classroom correspondence assignment into this curious 1925 anthology.
people.name: Sharpless Dobson Green

book: Compiled by Virginia jurist and educator James P. Holcombe for D. Appleton and Company in 1870, this anthology gathers nearly two hundred letters spanning three centuries of European and American letters—from Madame de Sévigné, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, and Samuel Pepys to Benjamin Franklin, William Cowper, and Charles Lamb.
Arranged around manners, art, criticism, biography, history, and morals, it treats the private letter as a literary form in its own right.

people.bio: Virginia legal scholar, educator, and anthologist who edited this 1870 survey of epistolary prose.
people.name: James P. Holcombe

book: Written between 1817 and 1844 from Marlow, Italy (Pisa, Leghorn, the Baths of Lucca, Rome, and Genoa), and London, these thirty-six letters—most addressed to Leigh Hunt and his wife Marianne—record Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley's daily reading, travels with Percy Bysshe Shelley, bereavement, literary friendships, and later efforts to edit Shelley's prose.

Henry Howard Harper introduced and annotated the manuscripts for a private edition of one hundred and fifty copies printed in 1918 at the Plimpton Press for Edmund D. Brooks of Minneapolis under the auspices of the Bibliophile Society.

people.bio: English novelist, essayist, and editor, author of Frankenstein, whose letters here chronicle life in England and Italy alongside Percy Bysshe Shelley and her widowhood work preserving his writings.
people.name: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley

people.bio: English poet, essayist, and editor of The Examiner who championed the younger Romantics and received many of Mary Shelley's letters from Italy and England.
people.name: Leigh Hunt

people.bio: Silhouette artist and sculptor, wife of Leigh Hunt, and close friend and frequent confidante of Mary Shelley.
people.name: Marianne Hunt

people.bio: Bibliophile Society officer, author, and editor who wrote the introduction and notes to this 1918 collection.
people.name: Henry Howard Harper

book: Across more than two hundred letters and papers translated and edited by Robert W. Carden in 1913 (Houghton Mifflin), Michelangelo appears far from marble myth: haggling over Carrara quarries, wrangling with patrons and popes over the Sistine Chapel and Julius II’s tomb, lecturing his nephew Lionardo on marriage and thrift, and grieving the death of his servant Urbino.
Read in sequence, the correspondence forms an unvarnished self-portrait of a working artist across nearly seventy years.

people.bio: Florentine sculptor, painter, architect, and poet whose surviving letters record seven decades of workshop life, family obligation, and papal commissions.
people.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti

people.bio: British writer and translator who edited and translated Michelangelo’s letters and papers into English for the 1913 Houghton Mifflin edition.
people.name: Robert W. Carden

book: John Stuart Mill’s letters from 1831 to 1863 trace a mind steadily outgrowing the rigid Benthamite mould in which his father raised him. Written alongside his thirty-five years as an examiner at East India House, they follow his intense intellectual friendships with Thomas Carlyle and Alexis de Tocqueville, his marriage to Harriet Taylor, and the gestation of On Liberty and Representative Government—always in prose of cool precision and rare fairness toward opponents.
Hugh S. R. Elliot edited the collection with a substantial biographical introduction for Longmans, Green and Co. in 1910, working from papers preserved by Mill’s stepdaughter Helen Taylor.

people.bio: English philosopher, political economist, and Member of Parliament whose books On Liberty and The Subjection of Women became cornerstones of modern liberal argument.
people.name: John Stuart Mill

people.bio: English scientific writer chosen by Mill’s literary executrix to prepare the first collected edition of his correspondence.
people.name: Hugh S. R. Elliot

book: In the summer of 1928, while his ten-year-old daughter Indira was staying in the hill station of Mussoorie, Jawaharlal Nehru sat in Allahabad and wrote her thirty-one short letters about the beginnings of the world. Starting with the cooling earth and the first stirrings of ocean life, he walks through fossils, early languages, tribes, river civilisations, and the Ramayana and Mahabharata—clear, affectionate, and never once talking down to a child.
First published in Allahabad in 1929, this small summer book became the rehearsal for the far larger prison letters Nehru later gathered as Glimpses of World History.

links.label: Letters from a Father to His Daughter on Wikipedia

people.bio: Indian independence leader, writer, and the first Prime Minister of independent India. Separated from his daughter by politics and prison sentences, he turned letters into a portable schoolroom.
people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru

book: In late 1692 the young classical scholar Richard Bentley—chosen to deliver the inaugural Boyle Lectures in London—wrote to Cambridge to ask whether the new mechanics of the Principia pointed to a Creator. Over four brief, dense letters (1692–1693), Isaac Newton answers Bentley’s questions about gravity, infinite space, and why the fixed stars do not collapse together—and drops his famous dismissal of gravity as an ‘innate’ action at a distance across empty space.
First printed posthumously in London in 1756 for R. and J. Dodsley from manuscripts preserved by Bentley’s executor, keeping the original eighteenth-century spelling and long-s typography.

people.bio: English mathematician and natural philosopher whose Principia Mathematica (1687) unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics. Nowhere else did he state his cosmological assumptions so plainly.
people.name: Sir Isaac Newton

people.bio: English classical scholar, Master of Trinity College, Cambridge, and first Boyle Lecturer, whose sharp questions drew Newton out of his usual reticence.
people.name: Richard Bentley

book: Between 1869 and 1876 Friedrich Nietzsche and Richard Wagner enacted the rise and breakup of modern Europe’s most combustible intellectual friendship. The early letters glow with the twenty-four-year-old Basel professor’s weekend visits to Wagner’s villa on Lake Lucerne and the planning of Bayreuth; by the end, mutual adoration has cooled into silence as Nietzsche pulls free toward his own philosophy.

Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche stitched the letters together with connecting narrative, Caroline V. Kerr translated them, and Boni and Liveright published the book in New York in 1921 with a sharp, irreverent introduction by H. L. Mencken. Readers should keep Elisabeth’s protective editing in mind—later scholarship showed how carefully she shaped her brother’s archive.

people.bio: German philologist and philosopher appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four. His years beside Wagner shaped The Birth of Tragedy; breaking with Wagner set his mature voice free.
people.name: Friedrich Nietzsche

people.bio: German composer and dramatist who saw in the brilliant young professor a public champion for Bayreuth—and struggled when his disciple refused to remain one.
people.name: Richard Wagner

people.bio: American critic and journalist whose 1921 introduction frames the correspondence with characteristic scepticism.
people.name: H. L. Mencken

book: Before the telephone thinned out daily correspondence, the familiar letter was the freest form in English prose. This generous anthology gathers over three hundred letters from William Blake, Jane Austen, Charles Lamb, and John Keats through the Brownings, Charlotte Brontë, Dickens, Lincoln, Emily Dickinson, and Robert Louis Stevenson—full of gossip, jokes, money worries, grief, and writers thinking aloud among friends.
Selected and introduced by Byron Johnson Rees for Charles Scribner’s Sons’ Modern Student’s Library in 1919.

people.bio: Professor of English at Williams College who edited this anthology to catch nineteenth-century prose off its guard.
people.name: Byron Johnson Rees

book: Courtship, jealousy, longing, and long marriage across four centuries (1443–1844), arranged in three sections: Poets and Men of Letters, Royal Personages, and Statesmen and Men of Affairs. Inside are John Keats writing in fever to Fanny Brawne, Jonathan Swift’s coded baby-talk to Stella, Richard Steele’s rushed tavern notes to his ‘dear Prue’, Henry VIII wooing Anne Boleyn, and Oliver Cromwell writing quietly to his wife between campaigns.
Edited with short biographical headnotes by Abby Sage Richardson and published in Boston by James R. Osgood and Company in 1883.

people.bio: American writer, actress, and literary historian who edited classic English prose and verse for late nineteenth-century readers.
people.name: Abby Sage Richardson

book: Banished from Rome in late A.D. 8 at the age of fifty by personal edict of the Emperor Augustus—relegated for 'two offences, a poem and a mistake' (the Ars Amatoria and an undisclosed indiscretion; Introduction, scan leaves 22–28, pp. xviii–xxiv; scan leaf 38, p. xxxiv)—Publius Ovidius Naso (43 B.C.–A.D. 17/18) spent his remaining years at Tomis (modern Constanța), a frontier Greek port on the western shore of the Black Sea among Getic and Sarmatian tribes (scan leaves 30–34, pp. xxvi–xxx). From that bleak exile he sent back two collections of elegiac verse-epistles totaling ninety-six poems: the five books of Tristia ('Sorrows', 50 elegies, A.D. 8–12; scan leaves 49–309 odd, pp. 1–261), withholding the names of living Roman friends lest correspondence endanger them while addressing Book II directly to Augustus as a 578-line literary defence (scan leaves 105–147 odd, pp. 57–99); and the four books of Epistulae ex Ponto ('Letters from the Black Sea', 46 epistles, A.D. 12–16; scan leaves 311–537 odd, pp. 263–489), openly naming his Roman correspondents—Brutus, Paullus Fabius Maximus, Marcus Aurelius Cotta Maximus, Marcus Valerius Messalinus, Publius Pomponius Graecinus, Curtius Atticus, Sextus Pompeius, Germanicus Caesar, Albinovanus Pedo, his wife, and fellow poets.

Prepared from the first impression published in 1924 (London: William Heinemann; New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, MCMXXIV; title leaf, scan leaf 7; colophon, scan leaf 559, p. 511), this English prose translation and critical apparatus are the work of Arthur Leslie Wheeler (1871–1932), Alumnae Professor of Latin at Bryn Mawr College. The edition includes the Table of Contents (scan leaf 9, p. v), Wheeler's historical and manuscript Introduction with Selected Bibliography (scan leaves 11–48, pp. vii–xliv), all ninety-six poems of Tristia Books I–V and Ex Ponto Books I–IV with explanatory footnotes (scan leaves 49–537 odd, pp. 1–489), and the analytical Index of proper names and subjects (scan leaves 539–559, pp. 491–511).

people.bio: Roman elegiac poet born at Sulmo (Sulmona) on March 20, 43 B.C., of equestrian rank (Introduction, scan leaf 11, p. vii; Tristia IV. x, scan leaves 245–255, pp. 197–207). Celebrated at Rome for the Amores, Heroides, Ars Amatoria, Metamorphoses, and Fasti, he was relegated by Augustus in A.D. 8 to Tomis on the Black Sea, where he composed the Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto and died c. A.D. 17.
people.name: Publius Ovidius Naso (Ovid)

people.bio: First Roman emperor (r. 27 B.C.–A.D. 14), who relegated Ovid to Tomis by personal imperial edict in A.D. 8 without confiscating his property or civic rights (Introduction, scan leaves 21–28, pp. xvii–xxiv) and to whom Ovid addressed the single book-length plea of Tristia Book II (scan leaves 105–147 odd, pp. 57–99; Index, scan leaf 541, p. 493).
people.name: Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus (Augustus)

people.bio: Roman patrician, orator, consul of 11 B.C., and trusted confidant of Augustus, in whose household Ovid's third wife had been brought up alongside Fabius's wife Marcia (Introduction, scan leaves 16–17, pp. xii–xiii). Ovid addressed Ex Ponto I. ii and III. iii (and possibly III. viii) to him and mourned his sudden death in Ex Ponto IV. vi (scan leaf 489, p. 441).
people.name: Paullus Fabius Maximus

people.bio: Elder son of the orator and literary patron Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus, Roman soldier, orator, and consul of 3 B.C., to whom Ovid addressed Ex Ponto I. vii and II. ii and probably Tristia IV. iv (Introduction, scan leaf 16, p. xii; Index, scan leaf 551, p. 503).
people.name: Marcus Valerius Messalinus

people.bio: Younger son of Messalla Corvinus (adopted into the Aurelii Cottae), poet, orator, and loyal friend in whose suite on Elba Ovid was staying when news of his banishment arrived (Introduction, scan leaves 16, 29, pp. xii, xxv). Ovid addressed six Pontic Epistles to him (Ex Ponto I. v, I. ix, II. iii, II. viii, III. ii, III. v; Index, scan leaf 544, p. 496).
people.name: Marcus Aurelius Cotta Maximus

people.bio: Steadfast Roman friend and literary executor of Ovid (otherwise unknown outside Ovid's exile poetry), who edited the exiled poet's books at Rome and to whom Ovid dedicated the proem and epilogue of Ex Ponto Books I–III (I. i, scan leaf 313, p. 265; III. ix, scan leaf 467, p. 419) as well as Ex Ponto IV. vi and probably Tristia III. iv (Introduction, scan leaves 18–19, 39, pp. xiv–xv, xxxv; Index, scan leaf 542, p. 494).
people.name: Brutus

people.bio: Roman senator, soldier, patron of letters, and brother of Lucius Pomponius Flaccus; consul suffectus in May A.D. 16 and long-standing friend from the time of Ovid's Amores, to whom Ovid addressed Ex Ponto I. vi, II. vi, and the consular congratulation IV. ix (Introduction, scan leaf 17, p. xiii; scan leaf 503, p. 455; Index, scan leaf 547, p. 499).
people.name: Publius Pomponius Graecinus

people.bio: Intimate Roman friend and literary critic of Ovid who remained loyal after the poet's disgrace; recipient of Ex Ponto II. iv and II. vii (scan leaves 387, 397, pp. 339, 349) and probably Tristia V. iv (Introduction, scan leaves 18–19, pp. xiv–xv; Index, scan leaf 541, p. 493).
people.name: Curtius Atticus

people.bio: Wealthy Roman consular descended from an uncle of Pompey the Great and friend of Germanicus, who safeguarded Ovid's journey into exile and received four epistles in Ex Ponto Book IV (IV. i, IV. iv, IV. v, IV. xv; Introduction, scan leaf 17, p. xiii; Index, scan leaf 554, p. 506).
people.name: Sextus Pompeius

people.bio: Son of the elder Drusus, nephew and adoptive son of Tiberius, and poet-general whose intercession Ovid sought in later exile, addressing Ex Ponto II. i to him on Tiberius's Pannonian triumph and re-dedicating the Fasti to him (Introduction, scan leaves 19–20, pp. xv–xvi; scan leaf 367, p. 319; Index, scan leaf 546, p. 498).
people.name: Germanicus Julius Caesar

people.bio: Augustan epic poet and epigrammatist who served as cavalry commander under Germanicus on the North Sea campaign and received Ex Ponto IV. x comparing Ovid's endurance at Tomis to Ulysses' wanderings (scan leaf 511, p. 463; Index, scan leaf 540, p. 492).
people.name: Albinovanus Pedo

people.bio: American classical scholar, Alumnae Professor of Latin at Bryn Mawr College (and later Professor of Latin at Princeton University), who edited the Latin text and authored the English translation, historical Introduction, and critical notes for this 1924 edition of Ovid's Tristia and Ex Ponto (title leaf, scan leaf 7).
people.name: Arthur Leslie Wheeler

book: Alongside his shorter scientific and philosophical essays—On the Geometrical Spirit, the Preface to the Treatise on Vacuum, and On the Passion of Love—this volume gathers Blaise Pascal’s surviving private letters (1643–1660) to his sisters Gilberte and Jacqueline and his brother-in-law Florin Périer, including the stark, steadying letter he wrote on the death of his father.

George Pearce translated the book in London in 1849 from Armand-Prosper Faugère’s Paris edition, the first to restore Pascal’s writings straight from the manuscripts after two centuries of editorial smoothing.

people.bio: French mathematician, physicist, inventor, and Christian thinker whose experiments on barometric pressure and probability sit beside some of the tautest prose in French.
people.name: Blaise Pascal

people.bio: French archivist whose 1844 manuscript edition returned Pascal’s jagged, authentic texts to print.
people.name: Armand-Prosper Faugère

book: Printed in secret and hawked across Paris between January 1656 and March 1657 under the pen name ‘Louis de Montalte’, Blaise Pascal’s eighteen Provincial Letters began as a defence of the Jansenist theologian Antoine Arnauld and turned into one of Europe’s sharpest satires. Posing as a curious layman writing to a friend in the provinces, Pascal lets Jesuit casuists condemn themselves in their own words—inventing, almost in passing, the clarity and speed of modern French prose.
Translated by George Pearce for Longman in London in 1847, opening with Abel-François Villemain’s critical essay on Pascal as writer and moralist, with contemporary replies in the appendix.

people.bio: Turning from mathematics to polemic after his 1654 religious conversion, Pascal wrote the Provincial Letters at white heat; Voltaire later called them the first work of genius in French prose.
people.name: Blaise Pascal

people.bio: French literary historian, critic, and Minister of Public Instruction whose essay on Pascal opens this 1847 edition.
people.name: Abel-François Villemain

book: Between December 1810 and April 1811, eighteen-year-old Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote rapidly from Field Place, Horsham, and London to his Oxford friend Thomas Jefferson Hogg—arguing religious skepticism, recounting his engagement break with Harriet Grove, reacting to his expulsion from University College over The Necessity of Atheism, and reporting early negotiations with his father in London.
William Michael Rossetti and Harry Buxton Forman edited and annotated Volume I in London in 1897 in a privately printed edition limited to thirty copies.

people.bio: English Romantic poet writing here at eighteen during his Oxford term and the weeks immediately following his expulsion in spring 1811.
people.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley

people.bio: Barrister, writer, and Shelley's close University College confidant, co-expelled from Oxford in March 1811 and later author of a celebrated life of Shelley.
people.name: Thomas Jefferson Hogg

people.bio: Father of Thomas Jefferson Hogg (as identified on scan leaf 82, footnote to Letter XIV), to whom Shelley wrote in April 1811 regarding settlement terms.
people.name: John Hogg

people.bio: English man of letters, co-founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, and joint editor with H. Buxton Forman of these annotated 1897 volumes.
people.name: William Michael Rossetti

people.bio: English bibliographer and Shelley scholar who co-edited this privately printed annotated edition with W. M. Rossetti.
people.name: Harry Buxton Forman

book: Arranged in chronological order rather than traditional manuscript sequence (Table of Contents, scan leaf 9; Introduction, scan leaf 11, p. 1), the thirteen epistles transmitted under the name of Plato (427–347 B.C.; Chronological Table, scan leaf 23, p. 13) center on the dramatic entanglement of Athenian philosophy with Syracusan politics between 367 and 350 B.C. Beginning with the chatty court letter to Dionysius II after Plato's second Sicilian journey (Epistle XIII, 366 B.C., scan leaf 28, p. 18) and continuing through Epistles II, XI, X, IV, and III to the monumental autobiographical apology and philosophical digression addressed to the friends of the assassinated Dion (Epistle VII, 353 B.C., scan leaves 71–123, pp. 61–113), the constitutional counsel of Epistle VIII (352 B.C., scan leaf 126, p. 116), and the late letter of friendship to Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus (Epistle VI, 350 B.C., scan leaf 137, p. 127), the volume concludes with the four letters classed by the translator as spurious—Epistles I, V, IX, and XII (scan leaves 140–147, pp. 130–137).

Classical scholar Levi Arnold Post (1889–1971), then Assistant-Professor of Greek at Haverford College, prepared this English translation with a general Introduction, Tables of References, Chronology, and Descent, separate historical introductions to the individual epistles, critical endnotes, and an Index of Proper Names (Oxford: At the Clarendon Press, 1925; scan leaves 5–9). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Post's analytical bracketed summaries, Stephanus marginal references (309a–363e), polytonic Greek citations, and commentary verbatim (with printed pages 158–159 of the backmatter Notes—omitted by a camera double-leaf turn between scan leaves 167 and 168 in the primary Rollins College scan thirteenepistles0000plat—collated verbatim from Internet Archive second witness dli.ernet.247526, leaves n168–n169).

Source Text & Copyright Provenance: Translated with Introduction and Notes by Levi Arnold Post (Oxford: At the Clarendon Press, 1925; digitized at Internet Archive as thirteenepistles0000plat). Published in 1925, this work is in the public domain in the United States. Readers accessing this edition from jurisdictions governed by author life-plus-seventy-years copyright terms (Post, 1889–1971) should observe applicable local copyright laws.

people.bio: Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates, and founder of the Academy (Chronological Table, scan leaf 23, p. 13), whose three journeys to Syracuse in 388, 367, and 361 B.C. and alliance with Dion form the central subject of the thirteen Platonic epistles.
people.name: Plato

people.bio: American classical scholar and longtime Professor of Greek at Haverford College (title leaf, scan leaf 5), translator of the Thirteen Epistles of Plato (1925) and later editor of Menander and scholar of Greek drama and Plato's Laws.
people.name: Levi Arnold Post

people.bio: Son of Dionysius I and Doris (Tables of Descent, scan leaf 24, p. 14) who succeeded to the tyranny of Syracuse in 367 B.C.; recipient of Epistles XIII, II, III, and the spurious Epistle I (scan leaves 28, 37, 56, 140).
people.name: Dionysius II of Syracuse

people.bio: Syracusan statesman, son of Hipparinus I, brother-in-law of Dionysius I, and devoted disciple of Plato (Tables of Descent, scan leaf 24, p. 14), who overthrew Dionysius II in 357 B.C., received Epistle IV (scan leaf 51, p. 41), and was assassinated by Callippus in 353 B.C., prompting Epistles VII and VIII.
people.name: Dion of Syracuse

people.bio: Pythagorean mathematician, philosopher, and statesman of Tarentum who intervened with Dionysius II to secure Plato's safe departure from Syracuse in 360 B.C. (Epistle VII, 350a; Index, scan leaf 169, p. 161) and is the addressee of the spurious Epistles IX and XII (scan leaves 146–147).
people.name: Archytas of Tarentum

people.bio: Ruler of Atarneus and Assos in Mysia, patron of the Academic philosophers Erastus and Coriscus of Scepsis (Introduction to Epistle VI, scan leaf 137, p. 127), and later father-in-law and host of Aristotle; co-recipient of Epistle VI.
people.name: Hermias of Atarneus

people.bio: Pupils of Plato's Academy from Scepsis in the Troad whom Plato counselled in Epistle VI (scan leaf 137, p. 127) to form a philosophical bond of friendship with their neighbor Hermias of Atarneus.
people.name: Erastus and Coriscus of Scepsis

people.bio: King of Macedon (365–359 B.C.), elder brother of Philip II, and patron of Plato's pupil Euphraeus of Oreus; addressee of the spurious Epistle V (scan leaf 143, p. 133).
people.name: Perdiccas III of Macedon

people.bio: Mathematician of Thasos associated with Plato's Academy who sought Plato's help in framing laws for a newly founded Thracian colony, receiving Epistle XI in 360 B.C. (scan leaf 47, p. 37).
people.name: Laodamas of Thasos

people.bio: Loyal philosophical companion of Dion during the Syracusan civil strife, commended by Plato for his steadfastness in Epistle X (356 B.C., scan leaf 50, p. 40).
people.name: Aristodorus

book: Covering Books I–VI of the correspondence of Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus (Pliny the Younger, A.D. 61/62–c. 113; scan leaf 17, p. xi), Volume I of this two-volume edition presents 150 letters spanning Rome under Nerva and Trajan: senatorial trials such as the prosecution of Marius Priscus (Book II. xi, scan leaves 145–157), literary circles, villas in Tuscany and Laurentum, domestic life, and the two celebrated eyewitness letters to Cornelius Tacitus on the eruption of Mount Vesuvius and the death of the elder Pliny (Book VI. xvi, scan leaves 497–505, and VI. xx, scan leaves 511–519).

William Melmoth's classic eighteenth-century English translation (first published 1746) was revised by classical scholar Winifred Margaret Lambart Hutchinson (1868–1937) and first printed in 1915 (prepared here from the unmodified 1931 impression of the 1915 edition; title and imprint leaves, scan leaves 9–10). Volume I includes the Preface (pp. v–vii, scan leaves 11–13), Table of Contents (p. ix, scan leaf 15), Hutchinson's Introduction on Pliny's life, letters, and manuscripts (pp. xi–xvi, scan leaves 17, 20), and the English translations of Books I–VI (scan leaves 23–557 odd). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Melmoth and Hutchinson's historical orthography, small-caps openings, textual footnotes, and epistolary headers verbatim.

Source Text: Prepared from the unmodified 1931 impression (title leaf MCMXXXI, scan leaf 9; imprint verso 'First Printed 1915. / Reprinted 1923. / Reprinted 1927. / Reprinted 1931.', scan leaf 10) of the 1915 edition translated by William Melmoth (1710–1799) and revised by W. M. L. Hutchinson (1868–1937).

people.bio: Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, Roman lawyer, senator, consul (A.D. 100), and nephew and adopted heir of Pliny the Elder (scan leaf 17, p. xi), whose nine books of literary letters chronicle Roman public and private life under Nerva and Trajan.
people.name: Pliny the Younger

people.bio: English man of letters and translator whose 1746 translation of Pliny's Letters was praised as an English classic and served as the basis for W. M. L. Hutchinson's 1915 revised edition (scan leaf 9).
people.name: William Melmoth

people.bio: Winifred Margaret Lambart Hutchinson, British classical scholar who revised William Melmoth's translation and wrote the Introduction for the 1915 two-volume edition of Pliny's Letters (scan leaves 9, 17–22).
people.name: W. M. L. Hutchinson

people.bio: Roman historian and senator, close friend and literary correspondent of Pliny, to whom Pliny addressed the accounts of the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Book VI. xvi and xx (scan leaf 501) as well as the prosecution of Marius Priscus.
people.name: Publius Cornelius Tacitus

people.bio: Roman biographer and scholar ('Lives of the Caesars'), friend and protégé of Pliny, for whom Pliny sought to purchase a small farm near Rome in Book I. xxiv (scan leaf 109).
people.name: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus

people.bio: Roman knight of Comum and grandfather of Pliny's wife Calpurnia, to whom Pliny wrote Book IV. i on his visit to Tifernum-upon-the-Tiber (scan leaf 295).
people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Fabatus

book: Volume II of Pliny the Younger's Letters (Books VII–X), translated by William Melmoth (1746) and revised by Winifred Margaret Lambart Hutchinson (1915), spans Pliny's late senatorial correspondence in Rome and his celebrated official dispatches as imperial governor of Bithynia and Pontus to the Emperor Trajan (Book X, c. A.D. 109–113), including Trajan's replies on municipal finance, building projects, civic privileges, and the treatment of Christians.

This volume (first printed 1915; 1927 impression on scan leaves 9–10) contains Book VII (scan leaf 13), Book VIII (scan leaf 103), Book IX (scan leaf 187), Book X (scan leaf 285), a Biographical Index of notable persons addressed or mentioned by Pliny (scan leaves 447–452), and an Index Siglorum of manuscript witnesses and early printed editions (scan leaf 452). This Paper Lanterns edition preserves Melmoth and Hutchinson's English translation, historical footnotes, small-caps headings, and epistolary layouts verbatim from the 400 PPI continuous-tone scans.

people.bio: Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, Roman lawyer, author, consul (A.D. 100), and imperial legate of Bithynia and Pontus under Trajan, whose ten books of Letters are a primary monument of Silver Age Latin prose and Roman provincial administration.
people.name: Pliny the Younger

book: Before the raven and the legend, there was a proud, penniless young man writing desperately to the Richmond merchant who had raised him without ever formally adopting him. These thirty-five letters from 1826 to 1833 follow the slow rupture between Edgar Allan Poe and John Allan across gambling debts at the University of Virginia, secret army enlistment, dismissal from West Point, and hunger in Baltimore.

Kept sealed for decades in the Valentine Museum in Richmond, Virginia, the correspondence was first published in full in 1925 by J. B. Lippincott with commentary and surviving school bills edited by Mary Newton Stanard.

people.bio: American poet, critic, and pioneer of the short story and detective tale. These early letters catch him before fame—alternately defiant, contrite, and broke.

book: In the autumn of 1848—a year after his wife Virginia’s death and a year before his own in Baltimore—Edgar Allan Poe courted the Providence poet Sarah Helen Whitman in eleven feverish, eloquent letters. Torn between romantic ardour, terror of relapse, and the opposition of Whitman’s family, they read like a late Poe poem spoken directly to a living listener.
James A. Harrison edited the small volume for G. P. Putnam’s Sons in 1909 to mark the centenary of Poe’s birth.

people.bio: Writing during the last twelve months of his life, Poe carried the same haunted rhythm from his poems straight into his courtship letters.
people.name: Edgar Allan Poe

people.bio: American poet, essayist, and transcendentalist in Providence, Rhode Island, who ended her engagement to Poe in December 1848 yet defended his name for the rest of her life.
people.name: Sarah Helen Whitman

book: Written around A.D. 303 during a forced absence on "the affairs of the Greeks" roughly ten months after his late-life marriage in Rome in A.D. 302 (Introduction, scan leaves 39–41, pp. 35–37; Letter § 1–4, scan leaves 57–60, pp. 53–56), Porphyry of Tyre's philosophical letter to his wife Marcella—a Roman widow and mother of five daughters and two sons—unfolds a deeply personal Neo-Platonic consolation. Across thirty-five surviving sections (scan leaves 57–83, pp. 53–[79], breaking off abruptly where the Milan manuscript ends), Porphyry counsels Marcella not to grieve for his bodily absence, tracing the ascent of the rational soul toward the divine through the four cardinal virtues of faith, truth, love, and hope, and distinguishing inward purity of mind from outward sacrifice.

Lost for centuries until Cardinal Angelo Mai discovered a fifteenth-century manuscript codex in the Ambrosian Library at Milan in 1816 (frontispiece plate, scan leaf 6; Introduction, scan leaves 41, 53–54, pp. 37, 49–50), the letter received its first English translation in this 1896 London edition published by George Redway (title leaf, scan leaf 7). Classical scholar Alice Zimmern (1855–1939) prepared her rendering from Mai's text alongside August Nauck's Teubner edition, prefaced by an essay on late-antique Neo-Platonism by Richard Garnett, C.B., LL.D., Keeper of Printed Books at the British Museum (Preface, scan leaves 9–20, pp. 5–16, dated October 1895), and Zimmern's own historical Introduction on Alexandria, Plotinus, Porphyry, and his treatise (scan leaves 21–54, pp. 17–50).

people.bio: Tyrian Neo-Platonist philosopher (born Malchus, named Porphyrius by his Athenian teacher Cassius Longinus; scan leaves 36–37, pp. 32–33), devoted disciple, biographer, and editor of Plotinus in Rome, who married Marcella in A.D. 302 and addressed this surviving philosophical epistle to console and guide her during his journey.
people.name: Porphyry of Tyre

people.bio: Roman matron, widow of a friend of Porphyry and mother of five daughters and two sons, whom Porphyry wedded in Rome in A.D. 302 on account of her disposition suited to true philosophy (Introduction, scan leaves 39–40, pp. 35–36; Letter § 1–3, scan leaves 57–59, pp. 53–55).
people.name: Marcella

people.bio: English classical scholar, suffragist, and alumna of Girton College, Cambridge (title leaf, scan leaf 7), who produced this first English translation of Porphyry's Letter to Marcella together with a thirty-four-page Introduction on Plotinus and Neo-Platonism (scan leaves 21–54, pp. 17–50).
people.name: Alice Zimmern

people.bio: English scholar, author, and Keeper of Printed Books at the British Museum, who contributed the critical Preface comparing third- and fourth-century Neo-Platonic ethics with primitive Christianity (title leaf, scan leaf 7; Preface, scan leaves 9–20, pp. 5–16).
people.name: Richard Garnett

people.bio: Founder of Neo-Platonism, born at Lykopolis in Egypt and pupil of Ammonius Saccas at Alexandria, under whom Porphyry studied in Rome for six years and whose Enneads Porphyry arranged and edited (Introduction, scan leaves 29–37, pp. 25–33).
people.name: Plotinus

people.bio: Italian cardinal and philologist who discovered the lost Greek manuscript of Porphyry's Letter to Marcella in the Ambrosian Library at Milan and published the editio princeps in 1816 (frontispiece, scan leaf 6; Introduction, scan leaves 41, 53, pp. 37, 49).
people.name: Angelo Mai

book: Collected here from the public-domain historical appendices of the 1962 Calcutta edition of Collet’s Life and Letters are Raja Rammohun Roy’s principal public petitions, constitutional addresses, and late European correspondence (1823–1833) absent from the 1914 edition. They open in Calcutta with his 1823 Press Regulation memorials to the Supreme Court and King George IV, his celebrated letter to Lord Amherst pleading for chemistry, mathematics, and natural philosophy over scholastic routine, the 1830 congratulatory address to Lord William Bentinck on the abolition of suttee, the Brahmo Samaj Trust Deed, and the petition drafted for Mughal Emperor Akbar II.

From his final years in England come his complete surviving three-letter exchange with Jeremy Bentham on judicial reform and Panopticon (1828–1831), his April 1833 letter to Robert Dale Owen on religion and social reform, and his December 1831 letters to T. Hyde Villiers and the French Foreign Minister challenging passport barriers and proposing an international parliamentary congress to arbitrate disputes between constitutional states.

book: Sophia Dobson Collet spent years collecting documents on the Bengali reformer, linguist, and founder of the Brahmo Samaj, Raja Rammohun Roy (1772–1833), whose letters address press freedom, English education, constitutional reform, and comparative religion from Calcutta to Bristol.

Completed after Collet’s death and issued in this 1914 Calcutta second edition edited by Hem Chandra Sarkar, the volume preserves fourteen complete letters alongside her biographical narrative. For Rammohun Roy’s fuller public memorials and later-unearthed correspondence—including his exchange with Jeremy Bentham, his 1823 letter to Lord Amherst, his letter to Robert Dale Owen, and his 1831 passport appeal to the Foreign Minister of France—see the companion volume Letters, Petitions, and Public Addresses of Raja Rammohun Roy.

book: Dictated largely in old age from imperial field camps in the Deccan (1659–1707), the Ruq‘at-i-Alamgiri preserves the private Persian notes of the sixth Mughal Emperor, Aurangzeb, to his sons—especially Prince Muhammad A‘azam Shah and Prince Bidar Bakht—and to his grand vizier Asad Khan. Threaded with Persian couplets and dry sarcasm, they catch an emperor who micromanages forts, revenue, court manners, and baskets of mangoes even as he watches his empire—and his own strength—give way.
Jamshedji Hormasji Bilimoriya translated the 181 letters into English with historical notes for joint publication in London (Luzac & Co.) and Bombay in 1908.

people.bio: Sixth Mughal Emperor, ruling for forty-nine years (1658–1707) over the empire’s widest territorial span. His private letters reveal a sharp, suspicious, austere, and unexpectedly self-ironic voice.
people.name: Aurangzeb (Alamgir I)

people.bio: Parsi scholar whose 1908 English translation and historical notes remain the standard English reference for the Ruq‘at-i-Alamgiri.

book: No two writers could have been built more differently than George Sand—warm, prolific, socially hopeful, writing from her country house at Nohant—and Gustave Flaubert—solitary, monastic, agonising for a week over a single sentence at Croisset. Yet between 1863 and Sand’s death in 1876 they exchanged over three hundred letters of deep affection and tireless argument over whether art owes anything to humanity or answers only to itself.
Translated by Aimée L. McKenzie with an introduction by Stuart P. Sherman, and issued in 1922 by Duckworth in London and Boni & Liveright in New York.

people.bio: Pen name of Amantine Lucile Aurore Dupin—French novelist, memoirist, and republican—whom Flaubert addressed affectionately as ‘Chère Maître’ (‘Dear Master’).
people.name: George Sand

people.bio: Author of Madame Bovary and Sentimental Education, whose letters to Sand hold his funniest, bleakest, and clearest reflections on literary craft, solitude, and the Franco-Prussian War.
people.name: Gustave Flaubert

book: Robert Schumann’s letters follow him from a reluctant law student in Leipzig and Heidelberg (1828) through the founding of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, his exhausting four-year legal battle against Friedrich Wieck to marry Clara, his joyful recognition of the young Johannes Brahms, and the gathering shadow of his final illness in 1854. Written with the same impulsive lyricism as his piano cycles, they read like a Romantic novel lived in real time.
Selected and arranged in three books by the German musicologist Karl Storck, translated by Hannah Bryant, and published in London by John Murray in 1907.

people.bio: German Romantic composer and music critic whose quick, poetic eye made him nearly as vivid a correspondent as a composer of Lieder and piano music.
people.name: Robert Schumann

people.bio: Virtuoso pianist and composer whose secret courtship with Robert during years of her father’s opposition forms the emotional spine of this book.
people.name: Clara Schumann

book: A trim, sharp-eyed anthology of fifty-nine letters stretching from the fifteenth-century Paston family and Sir Thomas More to William Cowper, Horace Walpole, Samuel Johnson, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Jane Austen, Byron, Shelley, Keats, and Robert Louis Stevenson. The test for inclusion here is prose pleasure—cadence, humour, and the sound of a real voice talking on paper.
Edited with short biographical notes and an essay on English epistolary style by Claude M. Fuess for Houghton Mifflin at the Riverside Press in 1914.

people.bio: American historian, biographer of Byron and Daniel Webster, and longtime headmaster of Phillips Academy, Andover.

book: Composed after his retirement from Nero's court in A.D. 62 during the years A.D. 63–65 (Introduction, scan leaves 16–18, pp. viii–x), the Moral Epistles of Lucius Annaeus Seneca (4 B.C.–A.D. 65; scan leaves 15–17, pp. vii–ix) are addressed to his younger friend Lucilius, a Campanian eques and imperial procurator in Sicily (scan leaf 17, p. ix). Volume I presents Epistles I–LXV: philosophical letters moving from everyday Roman scenes—saving time (Epistle I, scan leaf 27), discursiveness in reading (Epistle II, scan leaf 31), crowds and gladiatorial shows (Epistle VII, scan leaf 53), the humane treatment of slaves (Epistle XLVII, scan leaf 325), Baiae, Vatia's villa, the din of the Roman baths, and the Naples tunnel (Epistles LI, LV–LVII, scan leaves 361, 389–397)—to Stoic reflections on friendship, old age, illness, and death, enriched with sayings of Epicurus and verses from Vergil and Publilius Syrus.

Volume I opens with Richard Mott Gummere's Introduction (signed Haverford College, May 1916; scan leaves 15–20, pp. vii–xii), note on the manuscripts following Otto Hense's second Teubner edition of 1914 (scan leaf 21, p. xiii), and Bibliography (scan leaves 22–23, pp. xiv–xv), followed by the English translations and explanatory footnotes of Epistles I–LXV (scan leaves 27–471 odd, pp. 3–459). Because the primary 500-PPI scan (adluciliumepistu01seneuoft, 1925 impression) physically lacks a twelve-page signature (pp. 371–382) between scan leaves 394 and 395, the concluding lines of Epistle LV and the entirety of Epistle LVI ('On Quiet and Study', pp. 371–381) together with their facing-verso explanatory footnotes are collated verbatim from the complete 1917 first-printing witness (bub_gb_pa1EAQAAIAAJ, leaves n387–n399).

book: Composed during Lucius Annaeus Seneca's retirement from Nero's court in A.D. 63–65 and addressed to his friend Gaius Lucilius Iunior, imperial procurator in Sicily, Volume II of the Epistulae Morales gathers Letters LXVI–XCII—some of the longest and most searching philosophical essays in the collection. Across these twenty-seven letters Seneca examines the equality of moral goods as exemplified by his crippled school-mate Claranus (Epistle LXVI, scan leaf 15, p. 3), the ethics of voluntary death (Epistles LXX and LXXVII, scan leaves 69 and 181, pp. 57 and 169, opening with the arrival of the Alexandrian mail-boats at Puteoli), scientific inquiry into Mount Aetna during Lucilius's Sicilian circuit (Epistle LXXIX, scan leaf 213, p. 201), austere republican simplicity written from the villa of Scipio Africanus at Liternum (Epistle LXXXVI, scan leaf 323, p. 311), the boundaries of liberal studies and technological progress against Posidonius (Epistles LXXXVIII and XC, scan leaves 361 and 407, pp. 349 and 395), consolation to Liberalis after the great fire that levelled Lugdunum (Lyons) in A.D. 64 (Epistle XCI, scan leaf 443, p. 431), and the self-sufficiency of the happy life (Epistle XCII, scan leaves 459–483, pp. 447–471).

Prepared from the 1920 printing containing the Title Leaf (scan leaf 9), Table of Contents (scan leaves 11–12, pp. v–vi), and Richard Mott Gummere's English translation of Epistles LXVI–XCII across 235 recto pages (scan leaves 15–483 odd, pp. 3–471), this Paper Lanterns edition preserves Gummere's historical orthography, indented verse translations, and explanatory footnotes verbatim.

book: Written during Lucius Annaeus Seneca's final retirement from Nero's court in A.D. 64–65 and addressed to his friend Gaius Lucilius Iunior, Volume III concludes the extant corpus of the Epistulae Morales with Letters XCIII–CXXIV. Across these thirty-two letters Seneca reflects on the death of the Neapolitan philosopher Metronax and the fullness rather than length of human life (Epistle XCIII, scan leaf 15, p. 3), develops his monumental twin treatises on ethical precepts and foundational Stoic doctrines (Epistles XCIV and XCV, scan leaves 23 and 71, pp. 11 and 59), appraises the philosophical prose of Papirius Fabianus (Epistle C, scan leaf 161, p. 149), recounts his retreat to his country estate at Nomentum with his wife Paulina alongside the examples of Socrates and Cato the Younger (Epistle CIV, scan leaf 203, p. 191), recalls his youthful asceticism under his teachers Attalus and Sotion (Epistle CVIII, scan leaf 241, p. 229), diagnoses corrupt literary style as a mirror of moral character through the case of Gaius Maecenas (Epistle CXIV, scan leaves 313–315, pp. 301–303), and closes the collection with the demonstration that human Good is perfected solely through reason (Epistle CXXIV, scan leaves 447–461 odd, pp. 435–449).

Prepared from the 1925 printing containing the Title Leaf (scan leaf 9), Imprint Leaf (scan leaf 10), Table of Contents (scan leaves 11–12, pp. v–vi), and Richard Mott Gummere's English translation of Epistles XCIII–CXXIV across 224 recto pages (scan leaves 15–461 odd, pp. 3–449), this Paper Lanterns edition preserves Gummere's historical orthography, indented verse translations, and explanatory footnotes verbatim (with six abraded left-margin words on scan leaf 317, p. 305 collated from a second 1925 witness, IA senecaadlucilium0003rich, leaf n316).

book: Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius (c. 430–c. 489 A.D.)—Gallo-Roman aristocrat, prefect of Rome, poet, and bishop of Clermont (Arverni) in Auvergne—was the preeminent literary chronicler of the twilight of Roman Gaul. Spanning the tumultuous decades when imperial authority fragmented under Visigothic and Burgundian advance, his nine books of letters provide an unmatched, firsthand window into late antique aristocratic life, diplomacy, religious leadership, and epistolary culture.

Ormonde Maddock Dalton (1866–1945), British Museum archaeologist and classical scholar, published this definitive two-volume first complete English translation of Sidonius's correspondence for the Clarendon Press, Oxford, in 1915. Volume I contains Dalton's comprehensive 160-page introductory essay, critical bibliography, list of correspondents, and the complete text of Books I–III (comprising thirty-nine letters). Transcribed directly from the 1915 Clarendon Press edition, this Paper Lanterns edition preserves Dalton's scholarly apparatus, Latin notes citing Luetjohann, Mommsen, and Hodgkin, period orthography, and the authentic spatial layout of late Roman letter-craft.

people.bio: Gallo-Roman senator, poet, diplomat, and bishop of Clermont-Ferrand whose letters and carmina provide the central literary portrait of fifth-century Roman Gaul in transition.
people.name: Sidonius Apollinaris

book: Gaius Sollius Modestus Apollinaris Sidonius (c. 430–c. 489 A.D.), patrician of Lugdunum (modern Lyon), son-in-law to the Emperor Avitus, and Bishop of Clermont in the Auvergne, was the pre-eminent man of letters in fifth-century Roman Gaul during the collapse of imperial authority in the West.

This second volume of O. M. Dalton's translation for the Oxford Library of Translations completes the epistolary corpus, comprising Books IV through IX. These 108 letters record Sidonius's episcopal ministry, his defense of Clermont against the Visigoths under King Euric, his correspondence with contemporary bishops such as Lupus of Troyes, Claudianus Mamertus, and Faustus of Riez, and the literary leisure and rural estates of the Gallo-Roman senatorial nobility.

Ormonde Maddock Dalton (1866–1945), keeper of British and Medieval Antiquities at the British Museum, published this English translation with introduction, notes, and index through the Clarendon Press, Oxford, in 1915. This Paper Lanterns diplomatic edition transcribes the volume verbatim from the University of Toronto (PIMS) copy, conserving inline Latin and Greek phrases, metrical verse inscriptions, and scholarly endnotes.

book: Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–c. 414 A.D.)—patrician landowner, Neoplatonist philosopher, devoted disciple of Hypatia, and later bishop of Ptolemais in the Libyan Pentapolis—left one of the most intimate, varied, and historically precious epistolary corpora of late antiquity. Spanning philosophical reflections, passionate defenses of his Libyan homeland against nomadic Ausurian raiders, public letters of church discipline, and affectionate personal correspondence, these 159 surviving letters offer an unmatched firsthand window into the intellectual and political world of fourth- and fifth-century Greek culture.

Augustine FitzGerald (1862–1930) produced this landmark first complete English translation of Synesius's letters, published by Humphrey Milford at the Oxford University Press in 1926. Transcribed directly from the 1926 OUP edition, this Paper Lanterns edition preserves FitzGerald's historical introduction, analytical notes citing Druon, Crawford, Petavius, and Hercher, and his verbatim renderings of classical Greek and Latin quotations, period spelling, and epistolary layout.

people.bio: Greek philosopher, pupil of Hypatia of Alexandria, and bishop of Ptolemais in Cyrenaica, whose extant letters, hymns, and treatises blend Neoplatonic philosophy with vivid depictions of late Roman provincial life.
people.name: Synesius of Cyrene

people.bio: Irish classical scholar and translator who produced the first complete English translations of the Letters and the Essays and Hymns of Synesius of Cyrene for the Oxford University Press.
people.name: Augustine FitzGerald

people.bio: Celebrated Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer, and mathematician at Alexandria, teacher and lifelong friend of Synesius, who addressed seven of his most famous letters to her.
people.name: Hypatia

people.bio: Patriarch of Alexandria (385–412) who consecrated Synesius as metropolitan bishop of Ptolemais and was addressed by him on church administration and pastoral discipline.
people.name: Theophilus of Alexandria

people.bio: Synesius' elder brother and most frequent correspondent, recipient of extensive letters concerning the defence of Cyrene, family affairs, and philosophical contemplation.
people.name: Evoptius of Cyrene

people.bio: Constantinopolitan advocate and close intellectual friend of Synesius, whom Synesius met during his three-year diplomatic embassy to the imperial court of Arcadius.
people.name: Pylaemenes of Heraclea

book: Between 1885 and 1895, in his twenties and early thirties, Rabindranath Tagore spent long stretches living on a houseboat on the Padma River while managing his family’s estates at Shelidah and Patisar in eastern Bengal. Writing home in Bengali to his niece Indira Devi—translated here under his own eye—he sets down monsoon clouds, sandbanks, village ferries, and the quiet solitude out of which his finest short stories emerged.
Published by Macmillan in 1921, Glimpses of Bengal preserves Tagore before the Nobel Prize and global lecture tours, when his attention belonged entirely to the rivers and seasons of Bengal.

people.bio: Bengali poet, songwriter, novelist, painter, and educator—the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913)—whose Padma letters (Chhinnapatra) are among the finest prose in modern Indian literature.
people.name: Rabindranath Tagore

book: A slim, rarely seen Macmillan booklet from 1917 gathering thirteen extracts from Rabindranath Tagore’s 1893 letters—written during the same rural Bengal years that later yielded Glimpses of Bengal. Moving between Calcutta, Cuttack, and the Padma sandbanks at Shelidah, these early English translations offer a brief first look at how Tagore let ordinary weather and river light open into quiet reflection.
Issued in New York by The Macmillan Company in 1917, four years before the fuller 1921 selection.

people.bio: Bengali poet and polymath whose 1890s letters from eastern Bengal first reached English readers through short selections like this 1917 booklet.
people.name: Rabindranath Tagore

book: Across the turbulent decade from 1913 to 1923, Rabindranath Tagore wrote over a hundred letters to Charles Freer Andrews—the English missionary and teacher who stood close to both Tagore and Gandhi. Written through the First World War, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the Non-Cooperation Movement, and exhausting lecture tours across Japan, Europe, and America, they lay bare Tagore’s dread of militant nationalism, his affectionate disagreements with Gandhi, and his hopes for his school at Santiniketan.
C. F. Andrews edited the letters and prefaced them with two introductory essays for George Allen & Unwin in London in 1928.

people.bio: After his 1913 Nobel Prize, Tagore found himself an uneasy public sage—torn between foreign lecture halls and his quiet campus at Santiniketan, a pull felt throughout this book.
people.name: Rabindranath Tagore

people.bio: English missionary, reformer, and teacher at Santiniketan whom Gandhi called ‘Deenabandhu’ (‘Friend of the Poor’). His loyalty bridged Tagore and Gandhi through ten difficult years.
people.name: C. F. Andrews

book: After Seringapatam fell and Tipu Sultan was killed in May 1799, East India Company officers carried off the Persian letter-books of the Mysore palace. These 431 state dispatches and orders (1785–1799)—addressed to fort governors, army commanders, commercial agents, and envoys to Constantinople and France—show an eighteenth-century Indian ruler running a tightly wound state: rocket batteries, silk and sandalwood monopolies, coinage, spies, and unforgiving discipline.

Major-General William Kirkpatrick, a veteran Company soldier and Persian scholar, selected, translated, and annotated the letters for Black, Parry, and Kingsbury in London in 1811. His adversarial British commentary sits right beside primary documents of rare administrative granularity.

people.bio: Ruler of Mysore from 1782 until his death defending Seringapatam in 1799, remembered for his iron-cased rockets, state trading factories, and relentless resistance to East India Company rule.
people.name: Tipu Sultan

people.bio: East India Company officer, Persian scholar, and military secretary to Lord Wellesley who combed the captured Mysore records to produce this 1811 edition.
people.name: William Kirkpatrick

book: By the 1890s Leo Tolstoy had largely set novels aside for a sterner vocation: radical Christian pacifism, manual labour, and open confrontation with the Russian church and state. Alongside late essays, this volume gathers twelve public letters (1893–1902)—including his calm reply to the Holy Synod’s excommunication, his direct appeals to Tsar Nicholas II, and his defences of conscientious objectors, arguments that soon reached and moved the young Gandhi in South Africa.
Translated by Aylmer Maude and published in London by Grant Richards in 1903 as Volume XLVI of The World’s Classics.

people.bio: Author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina whose late moral essays and open letters turned Yasnaya Polyana into a clearing-house for pacifists and dissenters worldwide.
people.name: Leo Tolstoy

book: Toru Dutt died of consumption in Calcutta in August 1877 at twenty-one, leaving behind translations from French poetry, a French novel, English ballads drawn from Sanskrit epics, and a stack of letters to her English friend Mary Martin in Cambridge. Written from her family’s town house and their mango-orchard retreat at Baugmaree, the letters are quick, funny, and full of life—horses, books ordered from London, Sanskrit lessons with her father, and sharp asides on colonial Calcutta.
Harihar Das tracked down her correspondence in England and France and wove it into this biography for Oxford University Press in 1921, with a foreword by H. A. L. Fisher.

people.bio: Bengali poet, novelist, and translator who mastered French and English during four years in Europe before returning to Calcutta to study Sanskrit and write Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan.
people.name: Toru Dutt

people.bio: Bengali historian and biographer who gathered Toru Dutt’s surviving letters to Mary Martin and Clarisse Bader to assemble this 1921 volume.
people.name: Harihar Das

book: Swami Vivekananda’s letters (1888–1902) move at a pace his formal lectures rarely match. Starting from his years as a wandering monk with no fixed address, they sweep through the 1893 Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago, winter train journeys across America, friendships in England, and the exhausting work of building the Ramakrishna Mission at Belur Math—alternately blazing with impatience, funny, tender, and bone-tired.
Issued in its fourth edition by Advaita Ashrama at Mayavati in the Himalayas in 1944, with biographical notes on the disciples and friends addressed across the book.

people.bio: Born Narendranath Datta in Calcutta; chief disciple of Sri Ramakrishna, philosopher of Vedanta, and founder of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission. He died at thirty-nine, leaving behind more than three hundred vivid letters.
people.name: Swami Vivekananda

book: More than twenty thousand of Voltaire’s letters survive—fast, lethal, and endlessly curious, serving as eighteenth-century Europe’s informal newspaper. This selection of ninety-one follows him from his cocky Parisian youth in 1713 through exile in England, scientific years with Émilie du Châtelet at Cirey, his souring stay at Frederick the Great’s court in Potsdam, and his vigorous old age at Ferney campaigning against judicial torture and religious intolerance.
Evelyn Beatrice Hall—writing under her pen name S. G. Tallentyre—translated the letters and linked them with crisp biographical sketches in 1919.

people.bio: Born François-Marie Arouet; French Enlightenment satirist, historian, and polemicist whose private letters often hit harder—and travelled faster—than his published books.
people.name: Voltaire

people.bio: English biographer of Voltaire—author of the famous summary ‘I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it’—who translated and framed this selection.
people.name: S. G. Tallentyre (Evelyn Beatrice Hall)
